title: I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists
excerpt: > The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.
content_html:
> The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

Fatal misunderstanding.

Datacenters are not warehouses. Amazon.com being borderline-profitable owing to massive ongoing capex on warehouse expansion is not at all like AWS becoming borderline-profitable owing to massive ongoing capex on LLM datacenter build-out and SOTA model training (it's CAPEX, but carries OPEX affect because of GPU depreciation schedules and competitive hardware upgrade cycles), and opex of delivering LLM inference services, and being able to price it all competitively.

(edit: expand explanation of why it's a misunderstanding)


There's also a failure to misunderstand the arms race nature of it all and the need to be in the lead since everyone is assuming it's a winner take all market. That's probably close to correct.

A data center is a warehouse for sure but the building is only a few percent of the cost. The GPUs are probably 80% of the total cost or more. And they probably only have a 3-5 year primary lifecycle.

Pay the building off over 20 years? Sure but 80% of your capex problems remain. 2 trillion already spent? Just those GPUs need to generate 500 billion a year over the next 5 years.


> everyone is assuming it's a winner take all market.

I guess this is the big gamble, the idea that if you just spend enough money as fast as you can you can become the gods of AI forever and can just charge whatever you want for your magic beans.

But what is the moat? If in reality these things become commodities and just compete with each other to spit out cheap tokens then there's no way the margins are there.


> everyone is assuming it's a winner take all market

I don't think anyone serious believes this any more. The tech is thoroughly commoditized. There are a lot of plays to be made, like OpenAI cornering memory, or spending heavily on unique data for RL, if you can stop distilling, but there is no proprietary core IP at all.

There is no way to monopolize a technology this big. It would be like monopolizing literacy.


It's not the AI technology itself that is being monopolized, it's the data necessary to train it.

More specifically: when everything you could previously have earned money with is subsumed by AI, the "frontier" of profitable knowledge exists solely with the highest concentration of capital. Because that's where the highest amount of compute and consequently valuable data is.

Already now the idea of the tech being "commoditized" is true only if you exclusively look at the bubble of rich countries. AI-worthy compute is prohibitively expensive otherwise for individuals.


Specifically with regards to the data necessary to train, the AI companies have allowed the earth to be scorched (to say scorched earth tactic is to attribute intent, which I wish to avoid for my point), making clean training data harder to obtain. Essentially, what I do see as intended is the enclosure of an intellectual commons.


You don't need clean data to train, just "reasonable" data. General bulk data from the wider world isn't the difficult part. AFAIU task specific RL environments, custom annotated datasets, and access to the raw compute necessary to actually perform the training are the primary limiting factors. The latter in particular is no joke. Most companies won't be able to afford the pretraining for a frontier sized model. Even "small" models can run into the millions USD IIUC.


> AI is simultaneously at the forefront of mathematics and unable to do accounting.

It's almost as if arithmetic were the least important part of mathematics. :-)


Power, natural gas, gasoline, water, mobile contracts, railways, internet access are probably better analogies. They have tendencies to (local) monopolies but also a lot of precedent and knowledge on how to regulate and break them, how to introduce competition.


I don't think so. You can't practically buy electricity from halfway across the planet but you can buy tokens. There's no local infrastructure to monopolise.


they broke up Ma Bell, but they've never done anything about the internet access. Mobile is an oligopoly.


The breakup of AT&T was the proximal cause of Ronald Reagan and Robert Bork installing the CWS shackles onto the US antitrust apparatus.

Here's the thing: we could remove those shackles. US antitrust law had a good 50 year run, it could have another. Lina Khan was working on it, you probably saw the flak. This was on the ballot in 2024 and it will be again in 2028.


> I don't think anyone serious believes this any more. The tech is thoroughly commoditized.

The latter doesn't imply the former. In other words it doesn't matter what the reality is, it matters what the excuses for sinking money down the hole are.

> There is no way to monopolize a technology this big. It would be like monopolizing literacy.

Again, I don't know if literacy is monopolized or not, that's a separate and quite long conversation, but whatever the case is, it doesn't mean anything wrt AI because GPUs and RAM are already monopolized and successful market scalping requires monopolization.

The bubble is simply an extraction mechanism, the conditions for it are present now, as are the will and power available to those who can do it and benefit from it. How long it's going to continue is a question with many unknowns but the conditions for it can be maintained for at least another 3 to 7 years.


I think the big gamble is the bet on recursive self improvement (RSI) and getting there first is assumed to be the moat. At least I think what is being sold is this to justify the huge investment on future returns. I personally think that the probability of that happening is pretty low, but investors are swayed by the enormous returns it implies. I guess we will see how it plays out in a few years time. Until then it is important to keep a cool head, experiment with the new tools, and keep your reasoning skills sharp. As someone who can not personally invest on RSI, I feel my only play is to bet on AI becoming a commodity and ready for that future. If that happens, a lot of these datacenter bets will pay a fraction of the expected returns, but we will have cheap cloud compute and local models for inference, an age of personal AI that mirrors the advance of personal computing.


The moat was "AI", as in, self-improving Superintelligence (Nick Bostrom-style). They thought they were _just_ on the cusp of this happening, thus hundreds of billions of dollars was small fry. At that point either your AI figures out how to make money, or money doesn't even matter.


> and can just charge whatever you want for your magic beans.

'Winner take all' doesn't mean convincing others to buy your product. If others have something to buy your product with, you've not taken all, fundamentally.

'Winner take all' means having the most powerful army. The assumption is that once AI crosses a certain threshold then there won't be anything the rest of us can do to stop the machine of whomever gets there first, so they will truly be able to take all. Hence why the AI labs sometimes hint about the risk of human destruction.


The army interpretation exists, and might sadly be relevant here, but it's not the only one. Google, for instance, won a nonviolent winner-take-all competition for search.


Different setup. IIRC, Google had fundamentally better tech than its competitors and was also the first to figure out search monetization.

With AI, it looks to me like competition is much tighter, with no company having fundamentally superior technology or monetization plan. So a winner-take-all scenario is much less likely.


You're right that Google has been greatly helped by having what has been considered the most powerful army (the US army) backing them. They wouldn't have had a hope in hell of surpassing the "mom and pop" stage without that.

But I am not sure you are right that it is powerful enough to secure all. I search daily, but cannot remember the last time I used Google. The other AI companies do it better. And I'm not alone in that sentiment. Google's stock price recently took a nosedive because investors have grown quite worried about the competition. Without a sufficiently powerful army stopping them, there will always be someone else ready to try to outdo you.


Google has class leading AI in virtually every category, owns a chunk of Anthropic, and is a landlord to both Anthropic and OpenAI. Plus Google's search ad business is still doing well, even if you don't personally use it.

Google shares dipped because AI shares dipped, not because their core business at risk. Google is in a _very_ strong position to capitalize on AI. Better than almost any other Big Tech company.


Google is doing very well, in large part thanks to it having a strong army behind it, but that's not anywhere close to being the same as having taken all. They have not done that. Not by any stretch of the imagination. Not even if you try to constrain "all" to mean search alone.


If Anthropic or OpenAI will take all using the most powerful army why they would give anything back to their investors? If that's a possibility than investing into AI companies is just gifting money to whoever will control this army.


Anthropic/OpenAI and the investors are the same thing. A company name is just a title for the people who own it.

Maybe you mean that you could see the employees of those companies (although I imagine they also own it, so that's a wrinkle) staging a coup to seize the army for themselves? That's certainly possible. They'd be in a good position to do so. Predicting the future is impossible, but if you want to be on the "right side" of that future army, owning its foundation today is still a reasonable bet.


After the IPO Anthorpic will have many thousands of investors, most of them will have no say in how the company will use its power. A coup by a small group of employees is also a possibility.


They mightn't have direct say, but the army would still be beholden to them (being on the "right side") under the current legal understanding. Of course, when the AI army takes over what we know today isn't apt to hold much water. A coup, as we established, is very plausible. However, as you cannot predict the future it isn't unreasonable to try to place the bet given what you do know. That's all you can really do. If you end up on the losing side in the end you'd also still be on that side if you didn't act at all, so why not take the chance if you believe one of these companies will eventually take all? The AI army, once it starts seeking all, is going to come and take your resources anyway.


> If others have something to buy your product with, you've not taken all, fundamentally.

Are you saying that winner-take-all markets are incompatible with capitalism? I'm confused


What suggests an incompatibility? Allowing private ownership of capital can absolutely support a winner-take-all situation. One private entity can own all the capital just fine, technically speaking. Many capitalism naysayers even use that situation as the canonical example of the peril of capitalism.

In reality the people would likely revolt by no longer recognizing private ownership of capital if that were to happen, but technically they don't have to. If they truly believe in capitalism — or, as it pertains to the discussion, there is an army forcing them to believe — they can continue to uphold the right for that private entity to own all the capital.


I take it you have a pretty specific perspective on capitalism, but most would say it can't really exist without a free market.


What is certain is that that we've never seen a free market in recorded human history. By the time the idea was invented we already had power structures in place that would never stand for a free market. Of course, the concept also has a number of unsolved practical problems which would prevent a free market from emerging in the real world even if everything else perfectly fell into place. Once markets were invented they were incorporated alongside existing systems, leaving the mixed economy we practice today the world over. An interesting thought experiment it is, but bold to think that private ownership of capital is dependent on that thought experiment. Especially given that most people seen here seem to believe that they actually can privately own capital despite the lack of a free market.

For the sake of discussion, if we entertain your thought, that means capitalism also doesn't exist beyond a thought experiment, which questions why it was brought into this discussion? Whether or not a winner-take-all-future is compatible with that thought experiment with no actual grounding doesn't mean anything, does it?


Mm.

If, and it is a big "if", someone were to become "the gods of AI", they get to perform a "pivotal act", i.e. take over the world. And if they do it wrong, end the world.

From the public statements, I get the impression that Zuckerberg is saying words solely to give positive vibes and does't actually believe any of that; that Musk might believe all of that but has only given as much cursory thought to it as one might get from reading a Wikipedia plot summary of Colossus: The Forbin Project, all The Culture novels, and an elevator pitch (~30 seconds or so) with Yudkowsky in 2013; others have certainly painted Altman in similar light; which leaves Amodei as a solid "C-" in the sense that while Anthropic still isn't taking this even close to seriously enough, he hasn't overtly said or done things that implicitly or explicitly show he thinks it's just fairy tales to get nerds interested in working for him.


A "failure to misunderstand" is a fitting turn of phrase.

People not only ignore second order effects, they also don't think about what would actually happen when a "winner" really "took all".

While AI is a tremendously useful technology, business types wildly misunderstand it and its consequences. Greed eats brain.


You got me on that one, geez! I'm not going to edit it though because I think you're right. Nobody really knows if there's going to be a winner-take-all or not. During the arms-race portion though people are definitely acting like it will be that way. But watching how fast models catch up to each other it's not obvious it will play out that way.


Thanks for the links!

The first one says that networking infrastructure costs 13% and the other says 1.5%. Not a great start.

Let's imagine that a traditional full rack can host 80ish H100s and that each one costs $25k. That's 2 million right there. There's probably only 10x cases in that rack so that's 10x dual core motherboards, RAM, network, etc. Call them 20k each. Maybe you need a 32 port 100gig fiber switch, that's 8k. Let's say it's 2.3 million per rack and 2 million of it is just the GPUs. We're at 85% of the rack cost right there in GPU, but the other stuff in the rack isn't durable either.

I suspect that it would take more than just another 100k per rack to finish out a data center so my "80% of the cost is in the GPUs" is definitely wrong. But I didn't see anything in these articles that indicated to me that 50% of the cost of a datacenter is anything really durable like buildings or electrical infrastructure or cooling. One rack might only take up 20ish sqft itself another 100sqft of isle. These buildings don't cost $10k/sqft to build the envelope. There's still an enormous amount of cost in stuff whose performance follows more of an exponential performance curve, not linear. It's just an absolute nightmare to try and amortize exponential performance curves with linear repayment.


These days there's usually two networks. Multi-trillion parameter models are too big to fit on one box of 8x H100's, so many of these are running RDMA (800Gb/sec on GB300 series) for rack-scale/many row-scale inference.

For GB300 series, pricing along the lines of $500k/server, 9 servers/rack ($4.5M/rack) before looking at water cooling, 800Gb RDMA network, and your 100Gb IP network


> since everyone is assuming it's a winner take all market. That's probably close to correct.

why? I keep seeing this over and over again but I've not seen an explanation. I would really appreciate some insight into this line of thinking, since it's not obvious to me. What is the benefit of holding hundreds of billions of computer hardware when it's not proven that it's even needed.


Lets say the total market for an arbitrary winner-take-all industry is $100 Billion/year in profits. Just so that we have a round number. And for another round number, lets assume the fair market PE ratio is 20x. This over-simplification would then have a fair market valuation of $2 Trillion total.

Just simple napkin math.

Now, lets say there are 5 companies competing to be the winner. Only one can be the winner, but all 5 are trying to be the winner. How much should each company individually spend?

Well... starting-bid is $2 Trillion, or ~$10 Trillion in the aggregate. Its basically the waste of competition. Because everyone is vying for monopoly power, the only fair for them to all invest over $2 Trillion in the hopes of being the dominant one at the end. Even if $8 Trillion is wasted, that's "other companies", your competitors, who lose out.

But wait: if one company spends $2.1 Trillion, that one company likely becomes the winner and the other 4 companies lose out. So then another company spends $2.2 Trillion, to get ahead of that war. Etc. etc.


I've read this 3 times and I think OP's question still stands. How is AI winner-take-all and not just a commodity market?

> Now, lets say there are 5 companies competing to be the winner. Only one can be the winner, [...].

Here you just stated what a winner-take-all market is, in the problem statement? Why can only one be the winner in AI's case? Even better: why can't they all be the losers if they spend as if this was a winner-take-all market? If one of the players suspects that's not the case, isn't it wise for them not to play the game as stated? What if ROI is logarithmic? What if the losing competitors go open source?

I have so many questions.

Is this a spherical cow?


> Is this a spherical cow?

Yes.

> I have so many questions.

I'm not saying this is correct. I'm just saying a lot of other people believe this. If they are wrong then they will lose a lot of money. If they are correct, most of them will lose lots of money but one of them will make money.

I agree with you that the chance of "everyone is a loser" is higher than the current Zeitgeist believes.


The idea is, innovation will concentrate where the necessary ingredients are.

When AI replaces human workers and researchers, the "frontier", with which you can earn money and gain an edge over your competition, resides in those data centers with the highest concentration of computational power.

If you own those data centers, you control the frontier of human knowledge, the edge where money and power is being carved out.


Power generation is also extremely expensive ongoing - either through gas turbines that eat fuel or on-grid power that datacenters will need to pay to capitalize (depending on ratepayer agreements of course - but clearly people aren’t stoked about subsidizing these)


In aggregate it’s a lot of electricity, enough to impact local grid markets.

But as a fraction of inference revenue, there is good reason to estimate that the direct electricity costs are perhaps 1-5% of inference revenue.

That’s a lot, but hypothetically if electricity prices double, it’s more likely to lead to angry residential consumers than a doubling of inference token prices.

Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, November 2026: https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-11...

There are substantial economies of scale on both power generation (grid-scale) and inference power consumption (batching and utilization).


That’s good to know and thanks for the links. I guess what I’m seeing is 5-7 year timelines on new construction, interconnect agreements, pushback on larger market rate agreements from FERC when states have new regulations, etc. In any case it will be interesting!

At this point it seems like data centers will not be able to share in their consumption and will be responsible for a lot of their generation costs. This might also impact the 5% number quite a bit if data center owners need to bankroll a 5 billion dollar plant then wait five years and then pay for its operation so investor-owned utilities can amortize the cost.


> That’s a lot, but hypothetically if electricity prices double, it’s more likely to lead to angry residential consumers than a doubling of inference token prices.

But that’s a feedback loop that could lead to more supply being built. Or it could lead to regulations that put enormous surcharges and low limits on data center power consumers, which effectively shield consumers directly from the lack of supply. Which in turn removes the incentive for consumers to expand power generation capacity to keep up (or to allow data centers to expand it themselves).

There is enormous opposition to a new data center project 30 miles outside my city because they want to build a 1000MW natural gas power plant and a 500MW biomass plant (that will take millions of acres of forest to sustain).

If that opposition continues, I see little chance of anything but electricity cost rising as a percent of inference.


Biomass powerplants use waste material as fuelnot fresh trees. They use waste wood like sawdust, scrap pieces. The most common fuel type is trash. They are used to recycle not to burn fresh resources.


I read somewhere that the expected 3-5 year lifespan of inference GPUs was not holding up to scaring: in practice, the GPUs have the same lifespan as any datacenter CPU or RAM. I think that estimate was based on Bitcoin mining ASICs, which wasn't an apples-to-apples comparison.


Older GPUs still have an active secondary market but they are probably not profitable at market rates for inference because newer chips are so much more efficient.

If Semi-Analyses is correct [1], even H100s would lose money at current prices - I doubt that is actually true of H100s in practice because from what I can tell it is based on a 3-year depreciation from the new price, but the point is that there is a point at which old hardware's operating inefficiencies dominate.

https://inferencex.semianalysis.com/infx/profit-estimator/de...


I'm not certain it's the longevity of the actual hardware so much as there is a huge incentive to replace your hardware with faster, more capable equipment. Who wants to invest in the AI company that's using 10 year old GPUs when the next company is using brand new?


Old GPUs today are selling and renting for more than they were new which suggests the typical depreciation pattern isn’t holding.

There’s a risk that likely will happen that once demand is met capacity will overshoot significantly. However, when will that occur is very up in the air. Everyone is training every larger models and there’s more AI usage than ever


There’s still a cost to underestimating asset depreciation from an accounting perspective. Imagine being left holding the balance sheet when you budgeted for X amount of depreciation but the demand drops significantly more than you expect during the next fiscal year. I guess my point is that artificially constrained supply is not a free lunch.


The problem is likely the GPU price, NVidia has a very large margin - but it doesn't seem like the the use case supports it. If NVidia cut the GPU price by 2-4x then these problems likely go away.

I wouldn't be surprised if most hyperscalers are betting on cheaper GPUs on their next upgrade through either pricing pressure on NVidia, competition from AMD/Broadcom or in-house chips.


> The GPUs are probably 80% of the total cost or more. And they probably only have a 3-5 year primary lifecycle.

There's plenty of data indicating that inference at typical API prices is profitable after accounting for the cost of GPUs. However that doesn't account for the arms race of training new models while performing R&D.


but is it a winner takes all market? currently we have models that are close-but-not-quite SOTA which are still heavily used and very profitable because they are _good enough_ (i'm talking about deepseek, of course).

or is the "winner takes all" mentality based on the assumption of being the first to achieve the technological singularity?


> or is the "winner takes all" mentality based on the assumption of being the first to achieve the technological singularity?

Alternatively, it may be based on becoming the favored provider of the defense or intelligence industries.


Normally you'd replace the device because there is more power efficient one on the market so running one at current energy prices costs more than buying new, more power efficient one and saving power.

IF prices of GPU/RAM come back to pre bubble costs, we might see the 5 year cycle of replacement that's relatively common in normal datacenters pre-ai bubble.

At current prices ? those GPUs that are there now will be running there in 10 years still.


> At current prices ? those GPUs that are there now will be running there in 10 years still.

If they don't burn out after two or three. Annualized failure rates are about 9% according to Meta.

A quarter will have failed within three years. Less than half of the original hardware will be running after ten years. In both cases if you assume that rate does not increase over time. Do H100s come with replacement guarantees?


I guess we will see. But I would not expect GPU hardware to last that long until there is some underutilisation in data centres.

Mind you, most of the H100s that have ever been sold are still in their packaging, I suspect. Or at least not plugged in.


Yep. Satya Nadella once quipped that they have GPUs sitting on shelves because they don't have enough power.

> [...] because quite frankly, the biggest issue we are now having is not a compute glut, but it’s power — it’s sort of the ability to get the builds done fast enough close to power. So, if you can’t do that, you may actually have a bunch of chips sitting in inventory that I can’t plug in. In fact, that is my problem today. It’s not a supply issue of chips; it’s actually the fact that I don’t have warm shells to plug into.

https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/artificial-intell...


I'm of two minds on this issue. Off the cuff I agree, but then again where are all the used "enterprise" GPUs coming from right now? There's plenty of secondary market for used Telas K, M and V series GPUs right now and the V100 is only 9ish years old, and that only if you bought it on the release day.

I do agree that 5 years isn't the hard cutoff I was suggesting but I'm not convinced that 10 years is a reasonable timeframe to consider paying the debt down when Moore's Law is involved. I know it's no longer the 12-18mo doubling it used to be but even if it's 2ish years then over 6 years you get 3 doublings or 8x performance gains. At 10 years it's another 2 doublings or 32x performance gains. It's hard for linear payback curves to deal with exponential performance curves past 2-3 doublings.


One thing that has to be considered with takes like this not assuming that things wont' get more efficient cost, power, or performance wise, when that's the only thing that's happened with hardware and software, ever.


Everything happening right now hinges on the idea that there's a singularity approaching.

If you think that, then all this greed and stupidity makes sense.

If not, well, it's just greed and stupidity init.


The gamble: gunning for market supremacy before investor cash dries up.

The real gamble: betting there is a large enough pool of c-suite that doesn't fundamentally grasp the concept of vertical integration that they're willing to pay to train their competition. Because if you think AI companies aren't training models how to do everything your company does with your data you are deeply delusional.

The real real gamble: praying sovereign governments stay anesthitized to the national security implications of a handful of extra-national organizations operating the conputer security equivalent of WMD with no oversight.


> And they probably only have a 3-5 year primary lifecycle.

I think in 3-5 years close to 100% of current GPUs/RAM will still be in service. New hardware matters only if gains in efficiency are large enough to put you out of business because the competition gets them. Extreme case of that are bitcoin miners. With AI inference there are way too many factors that influence the profitability. It's not like you can't run new model without the new hardware. It can just run on more of the old one. 3-5 years for GPU are estimates when the main application was gaming with new games with new requirements for running on a single GPU being constantly released.


You seem to be wrong about this

> A typical one-gigawatt AI data center requires $38 billion in up-front capital expenditure (CapEx) and $0.9 billion in annual operating expenses (OpEx). If CapEx is annualized over each asset’s lifespan, the total cost of ownership equates to $8.5 billion per year. Servers dominate this cost at $5 billion per year, or 60% of the total. Operating costs are small by comparison: even energy, the largest OpEx category, costs only $0.6 billion per year.

https://epoch.ai/data-insights/ai-datacenter-cost-breakdown


This is my heuristic for the capex split and effective lifetime of the asset it creates (I'm no expert of course, this is based on various reading):

- 20% Capex has ~20-year lifetime: The shell (land, building, cooling gear, rack mounts, power lines etc.).

- 80% Capex has ~3-year lifetime: The computers, including bulk commitments to power and maintain them.

And interest rates are why this split is a ticking time bomb. The sheer quantum of investment to build one is almost entirely debt funded (~90% of total outlay). I would guess the endgame would be bad even if the split for these entirely different asset classes is 50/50, which would be very generous, based on what I've understood.

Datacenter funding is extremely leveraged. For comparison, only some banks are allowed that much leverage for that size of capital, that too only if they have federal reserve backing. Even in such a case, the retail account holder (pseudo-investor, because our deposits are loans to someone else) has practically no downside protection. If the bank collapses you will lose everything.


Where are you getting the 20% and 80% split? The epoch.ai link suggests 60% is servers, which includes a lot more equipment than GPUs, so the 80% number is already off. It’s also unclear how power commitments is being included in that 80% with a 3-year lifetime.

In fact, to focus on the short lifetime assets alone, this more recent link suggests servers are 50% of CapEx, and GPUs are about 25 percentage points.

https://cib.bnpparibas/ai-infrastructure-investment-2026/

So already about 50% of CapEx spend is one-off construction / installation with a very long lifetime.

That leaves servers and GPUs. There is a ton of evidence out there that even chips from multiple generations ago, ie way more than 3 years old, are commanding pretty high rates. So even if they are replaced by newer chips every year, the older chips still hold a lot of value and can’t simply be written off to 0.

I think this is the most comprehensive look at the AI economy so far, probably a better source than the rest: https://www.exponentialview.co/p/the-state-of-the-ai-economy — it suggests everything is walking a tightrope but still sustainable for now.


> Where are you getting the 20% and 80% split?

Like I said, it's a heuristic, and the error bar on that opinion is... "50/50 split is also bad", for debt financing reasons. I'm skewing my guesstimate toward a pareto-split bear case, because 50/50 is the rosy-eyed best-ever case being proffered by parties who need the story to remain believable. I doubt anyone has a true grasp of the opaque financing as a single coherent picture.

In any case, I'm trying to reason from first principles.

A) The sheer quantum of debt financing skews the whole US economy, and that is a hard thing to skew. This means debt will keep getting repriced, higher interest rates, because risk exposure to financiers increases non-linearly when said risk becomes industry-wide.

B) Compute and power become inelastic, at the scale and rate of expansion of LLM datacenter. The become highly contested practically fixed resources. Prices will go up, and they are likely to go up faster with every marginal increase in demand.

C) Far better informed parties have been warning about severe under-quoting of liabilities for a while now. e.g. Some of the resources informing my opinion include publishing by Asad Ramzanali / Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator and Michael Burry / Cassandra Unchained. Worth reading their stuff:

After the AI Crash, by Asad Ramzanali, Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator (March 2026): https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6476159

Michael Burry Warns: AI Infrastructure Depreciation Is Masking Billions in Costs https://nova.kapualabs.com/goog-sys_onboarding/michael-burry...

(To be clear, just because Burry was spectacularly on the money that one time about CDOs, doesn't automatically mean he is right about this, but he does have a habit of calling out bullshit as he sees it, particularly dodgy financial engineering of the kind these people are doing... Corroborated by others like Asad Ramzanali.)


Ah, maybe "heuristics" is not an accurate word here, because it usually indicates something based in observation of empirical evidence or trial and error, even if its typically unscientific, so I was curious about the inputs to the 20/80 split.

I skimmed through the "After the AI Crash" paper, and it is really not an analysis but a policy brief that mostly reiterates, and uncritically accepts, a lot of the large numbers thrown about in other media sources. Interesting... Upon reflection, I feel like it's a "yes, and" proposition coming down to failure mode.

[Type A] Constant use a constant power level: Quantum world rules would dominate.

When run hot, electron tunneling will kill off individual transistors, and AFAIK that is a cascading failure mode once it takes root. A big enough failed spot, even if localised, could effectively kill a core (if not the whole chip---too many errors). A local hotspot will directly affect neighbours, and indirectly the chip as a whole because the same work is being pushed on fewer cores.

[Type B] Thermal cycled: Mechanical and electrical factors would dominate...

Microfractures / mechanical damage in weak areas of whole chips, and motherboards. In a hyperscaler server rack, if a board dies that part of the rack is dead---micro-maintenance is probably too expensive.

And speculating further, it stands to reason that Type B failures would likely cause Type A failures, and vice-versa.

Hyperscalers ... are ultimately profitable

Large data centers are dramatically more efficient at utilizing both the power and the hardware.

At it's core, running a top-tier LLM means linear load of trillion+ weights from RAM for every token. The cost of this operation absolutely dwarfs the cost of doing the actual math. If you are only serving a single user, you can only amortize this over a handful of token streams, times like 2-4 for speculative decoding. If you are running in a datacenter, you can batch thousands of streams, and get correspondingly much more tokens out of the same expenditure of energy and hardware.


Be slightly careful with this. Large datacenters use power to operate the facility (this is measured as PUE > 1). Datacenter-oriented hardware often contains low-diameter, high static pressure fans that consume quite impressive amounts of power that are not counted as overhead in the PUE calculation.

A home- or office-oriented workstation will have much less power-hungry fans (go compare a Noctua datasheet to a server fan datasheet - the Noctua wipes the floor with a server fan if measured by CFM/W, and the internal temperature rise is mostly controlled by airflow and not by static pressure). And in some climates and times of year the marginal facility HVAC cost associated with running a computer may be zero or even negative.

And lower utilization hardware may run in on a more efficient point on the power-vs-performance curve. [0]

That being said, your overall point is correct.

[0] For a dramatic demonstration of how much this curve matters, you can run a non-CPU-saturating, non-latency-sensitive workload on various Intel CPUs with and without turbo on. Seeing a 2x or greater difference in reported power is quite possible. (Intel is terribly at writing platform firmware and the default behavior may be wildly suboptimal.)

Just like some people will find creative ways to play the guitar while others will just play covers.By the way, you haven't addressed the core point posed: if people like AI output then is it still "slop" (in response to comments where people describe all AI output as "slop") Well, people also like junk food, does it mean it's not junk food anymore ?To me AI generated content is exactly like that. Cheap, fast and easy access.It's fine for occasional consumption, and in some setting it's definitely not suitable to be served High chance i will just talk to a meat proxy.The only way for them to prove themself to the mass is a live coding interview session, without AI of course > Behind it all is the Omarchy Doctrine: ten principles for...That's ridiculous... Let's vibe code everything, but with a doctrine and principles!If I'm going to do vibe coding, I don't need principles. No rules! And no future. "slop" is less so about if something is a popular product or not, it's more about the quality. You can think that AI can produce high quality outputs, but it's unreasonable to think that this applies to the majority of it's use. There has always been corner cutting, and using AI to cut corners/safe money in product design/production inevitably results already, and will more so in the future, in a ton of bad products. That does not mean that there can't be good ones too. > "slop" is less so about if something is a popular product or not, it's more about the quality.But we are talking about popular culture here. That was never an industry where quality was measured by artistic excellence. It's an industry that is entirely motivated by mass appeal. Thus something being popular IS the measure of success.So if AI is slop, then so is 99% of the human-made content it's replacing. Slop exists because the cost of creating content has dropped to zero, which made the signal to noise ratio crater as well. Concision and density used to be a virtue. Now it's the opposite: content is measured by weight. People absolutely cared about "C'était ça ou mourir", his publisher ended up dropping him. The reason the success continued is that people denied that he used AI and had all sorts of shaky political reasons for this (e.g. claiming that Haitian writing trips up AI detectors). Even the reason it got popular in the first place is to do with the themes of the novel rather than its writing. > his publisher ended up dropping himThat's not really the point. Critics the world over LOVED the book; they only distanced themselves from it when it became clear it was AI, but when they didn't know, they couldn't stop raving about it. most of the infrastructure will be garbage in 4 years. As before, it will become a monopoly of 1-2 big players and everyone else's datacenters will become ... crypto miners or something.

> The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

Fatal misunderstanding.

Datacenters are not warehouses. Amazon.com being borderline-profitable owing to massive ongoing capex on warehouse expansion is not at all like AWS becoming borderline-profitable owing to massive ongoing capex on LLM datacenter build-out and SOTA model training (it's CAPEX, but carries OPEX affect because of GPU depreciation schedules and competitive hardware upgrade cycles), and opex of delivering LLM inference services, and being able to price it all competitively.

It's not the AI technology itself that is being monopolized, it's the data necessary to train it.

More specifically: when everything you could previously have earned money with is subsumed by AI, the "frontier" of profitable knowledge exists solely with the highest concentration of capital. Because that's where the highest amount of compute and consequently valuable data is.

Already now the idea of the tech being "commoditized" is true only if you exclusively look at the bubble of rich countries. AI-worthy compute is prohibitively expensive otherwise for individuals.

The latter doesn't imply the former. In other words it doesn't matter what the reality is, it matters what the excuses for sinking money down the hole are.

> There is no way to monopolize a technology this big. It would be like monopolizing literacy.

Again, I don't know if literacy is monopolized or not, that's a separate and quite long conversation, but whatever the case is, it doesn't mean anything wrt AI because GPUs and RAM are already monopolized and successful market scalping requires monopolization.

The bubble is simply an extraction mechanism, the conditions for it are present now, as are the will and power available to those who can do it and benefit from it. How long it's going to continue is a question with many unknowns but the conditions for it can be maintained for at least another 3 to 7 years.

blocks.html_en: I think the big gamble is the bet on recursive self improvement (RSI) and getting there first is assumed to be the moat. At least I think what is being sold is this to justify the huge investment on future returns. I personally think that the probability of that happening is pretty low, but investors are swayed by the enormous returns it implies. I guess we will see how it plays out in a few years time. Until then it is important to keep a cool head, experiment with the new tools, and keep your reasoning skills sharp. As someone who can not personally invest on RSI, I feel my only play is to bet on AI becoming a commodity and ready for that future. If that happens, a lot of these datacenter bets will pay a fraction of the expected returns, but we will have cheap cloud compute and local models for inference, an age of personal AI that mirrors the advance of personal computing.

> and can just charge whatever you want for your magic beans.

'Winner take all' doesn't mean convincing others to buy your product. If others have something to buy your product with, you've not taken all, fundamentally.

'Winner take all' means having the most powerful army. The assumption is that once AI crosses a certain threshold then there won't be anything the rest of us can do to stop the machine of whomever gets there first, so they will truly be able to take all. Hence why the AI labs sometimes hint about the risk of human destruction.

blocks.html_en:
You're right that Google has been greatly helped by having what has been considered the most powerful army (the US army) backing them. They wouldn't have had a hope in hell of surpassing the "mom and pop" stage without that.

But I am not sure you are right that it is powerful enough to secure all. I search daily, but cannot remember the last time I used Google. The other AI companies do it better. And I'm not alone in that sentiment. Google's stock price recently took a nosedive because investors have grown quite worried about the competition. Without a sufficiently powerful army stopping them, there will always be someone else ready to try to outdo you.

blocks.html_en:
What suggests an incompatibility? Allowing private ownership of capital can absolutely support a winner-take-all situation. One private entity can own all the capital just fine, technically speaking. Many capitalism naysayers even use that situation as the canonical example of the peril of capitalism.

In reality the people would likely revolt by no longer recognizing private ownership of capital if that were to happen, but technically they don't have to. If they truly believe in capitalism — or, as it pertains to the discussion, there is an army forcing them to believe — they can continue to uphold the right for that private entity to own all the capital.

blocks.html_en:
What is certain is that that we've never seen a free market in recorded human history. By the time the idea was invented we already had power structures in place that would never stand for a free market. Of course, the concept also has a number of unsolved practical problems which would prevent a free market from emerging in the real world even if everything else perfectly fell into place. Once markets were invented they were incorporated alongside existing systems, leaving the mixed economy we practice today the world over. An interesting thought experiment it is, but bold to think that private ownership of capital is dependent on that thought experiment. Especially given that most people seen here seem to believe that they actually can privately own capital despite the lack of a free market.

For the sake of discussion, if we entertain your thought, that means capitalism also doesn't exist beyond a thought experiment, which questions why it was brought into this discussion? Whether or not a winner-take-all-future is compatible with that thought experiment with no actual grounding doesn't mean anything, does it?

If, and it is a big "if", someone were to become "the gods of AI", they get to perform a "pivotal act", i.e. take over the world. And if they do it wrong, end the world.

From the public statements, I get the impression that Zuckerberg is saying words solely to give positive vibes and does't actually believe any of that; that Musk might believe all of that but has only given as much cursory thought to it as one might get from reading a Wikipedia plot summary of Colossus: The Forbin Project, all The Culture novels, and an elevator pitch (~30 seconds or so) with Yudkowsky in 2013; others have certainly painted Altman in similar light; which leaves Amodei as a solid "C-" in the sense that while Anthropic still isn't taking this even close to seriously enough, he hasn't overtly said or done things that implicitly or explicitly show he thinks it's just fairy tales to get nerds interested in working for him.

blocks.html_en:
Thanks for the links!

The first one says that networking infrastructure costs 13% and the other says 1.5%. Not a great start.

Let's imagine that a traditional full rack can host 80ish H100s and that each one costs $25k. That's 2 million right there. There's probably only 10x cases in that rack so that's 10x dual core motherboards, RAM, network, etc. Call them 20k each. Maybe you need a 32 port 100gig fiber switch, that's 8k. Let's say it's 2.3 million per rack and 2 million of it is just the GPUs. We're at 85% of the rack cost right there in GPU, but the other stuff in the rack isn't durable either.

I suspect that it would take more than just another 100k per rack to finish out a data center so my "80% of the cost is in the GPUs" is definitely wrong. But I didn't see anything in these articles that indicated to me that 50% of the cost of a datacenter is anything really durable like buildings or electrical infrastructure or cooling. One rack might only take up 20ish sqft itself another 100sqft of isle. These buildings don't cost $10k/sqft to build the envelope. There's still an enormous amount of cost in stuff whose performance follows more of an exponential performance curve, not linear. It's just an absolute nightmare to try and amortize exponential performance curves with linear repayment.

Lets say the total market for an arbitrary winner-take-all industry is $100 Billion/year in profits. Just so that we have a round number. And for another round number, lets assume the fair market PE ratio is 20x. This over-simplification would then have a fair market valuation of $2 Trillion total.

Just simple napkin math.

Now, lets say there are 5 companies competing to be the winner. Only one can be the winner, but all 5 are trying to be the winner. How much should each company individually spend?

Well... starting-bid is $2 Trillion, or ~$10 Trillion in the aggregate. Its basically the waste of competition. Because everyone is vying for monopoly power, the only fair for them to all invest over $2 Trillion in the hopes of being the dominant one at the end. Even if $8 Trillion is wasted, that's "other companies", your competitors, who lose out.

But wait: if one company spends $2.1 Trillion, that one company likely becomes the winner and the other 4 companies lose out. So then another company spends $2.2 Trillion, to get ahead of that war. Etc. etc.

I have so many questions.

The idea is, innovation will concentrate where the necessary ingredients are.

When AI replaces human workers and researchers, the "frontier", with which you can earn money and gain an edge over your competition, resides in those data centers with the highest concentration of computational power.

If you own those data centers, you control the frontier of human knowledge, the edge where money and power is being carved out.

In aggregate it’s a lot of electricity, enough to impact local grid markets.

But as a fraction of inference revenue, there is good reason to estimate that the direct electricity costs are perhaps 1-5% of inference revenue.

That’s a lot, but hypothetically if electricity prices double, it’s more likely to lead to angry residential consumers than a doubling of inference token prices.

Lawrence Berkeley National Lab, November 2026: https://eta-publications.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2026-11...

There are substantial economies of scale on both power generation (grid-scale) and inference power consumption (batching and utilization).

That’s good to know and thanks for the links. I guess what I’m seeing is 5-7 year timelines on new construction, interconnect agreements, pushback on larger market rate agreements from FERC when states have new regulations, etc. In any case it will be interesting!

At this point it seems like data centers will not be able to share in their consumption and will be responsible for a lot of their generation costs. This might also impact the 5% number quite a bit if data center owners need to bankroll a 5 billion dollar plant then wait five years and then pay for its operation so investor-owned utilities can amortize the cost.

> That’s a lot, but hypothetically if electricity prices double, it’s more likely to lead to angry residential consumers than a doubling of inference token prices.

But that’s a feedback loop that could lead to more supply being built. Or it could lead to regulations that put enormous surcharges and low limits on data center power consumers, which effectively shield consumers directly from the lack of supply. Which in turn removes the incentive for consumers to expand power generation capacity to keep up (or to allow data centers to expand it themselves).

There is enormous opposition to a new data center project 30 miles outside my city because they want to build a 1000MW natural gas power plant and a 500MW biomass plant (that will take millions of acres of forest to sustain).

If that opposition continues, I see little chance of anything but electricity cost rising as a percent of inference.

I'm of two minds on this issue. Off the cuff I agree, but then again where are all the used "enterprise" GPUs coming from right now? There's plenty of secondary market for used Telas K, M and V series GPUs right now and the V100 is only 9ish years old, and that only if you bought it on the release day.

I do agree that 5 years isn't the hard cutoff I was suggesting but I'm not convinced that 10 years is a reasonable timeframe to consider paying the debt down when Moore's Law is involved. I know it's no longer the 12-18mo doubling it used to be but even if it's 2ish years then over 6 years you get 3 doublings or 8x performance gains. At 10 years it's another 2 doublings or 32x performance gains. It's hard for linear payback curves to deal with exponential performance curves past 2-3 doublings.

The gamble: gunning for market supremacy before investor cash dries up.

The real gamble: betting there is a large enough pool of c-suite that doesn't fundamentally grasp the concept of vertical integration that they're willing to pay to train their competition. Because if you think AI companies aren't training models how to do everything your company does with your data you are deeply delusional.

The real real gamble: praying sovereign governments stay anesthitized to the national security implications of a handful of extra-national organizations operating the conputer security equivalent of WMD with no oversight.

> And they probably only have a 3-5 year primary lifecycle.

I think in 3-5 years close to 100% of current GPUs/RAM will still be in service. New hardware matters only if gains in efficiency are large enough to put you out of business because the competition gets them. Extreme case of that are bitcoin miners. With AI inference there are way too many factors that influence the profitability. It's not like you can't run new model without the new hardware. It can just run on more of the old one. 3-5 years for GPU are estimates when the main application was gaming with new games with new requirements for running on a single GPU being constantly released.

This is my heuristic for the capex split and effective lifetime of the asset it creates (I'm no expert of course, this is based on various reading):

- 20% Capex has ~20-year lifetime: The shell (land, building, cooling gear, rack mounts, power lines etc.).

- 80% Capex has ~3-year lifetime: The computers, including bulk commitments to power and maintain them.

And interest rates are why this split is a ticking time bomb. The sheer quantum of investment to build one is almost entirely debt funded (~90% of total outlay). I would guess the endgame would be bad even if the split for these entirely different asset classes is 50/50, which would be very generous, based on what I've understood.

Datacenter funding is extremely leveraged. For comparison, only some banks are allowed that much leverage for that size of capital, that too only if they have federal reserve backing. Even in such a case, the retail account holder (pseudo-investor, because our deposits are loans to someone else) has practically no downside protection. If the bank collapses you will lose everything.

Where are you getting the 20% and 80% split? The epoch.ai link suggests 60% is servers, which includes a lot more equipment than GPUs, so the 80% number is already off. It’s also unclear how power commitments is being included in that 80% with a 3-year lifetime.

In fact, to focus on the short lifetime assets alone, this more recent link suggests servers are 50% of CapEx, and GPUs are about 25 percentage points.

https://cib.bnpparibas/ai-infrastructure-investment-2026/

So already about 50% of CapEx spend is one-off construction / installation with a very long lifetime.

That leaves servers and GPUs. There is a ton of evidence out there that even chips from multiple generations ago, ie way more than 3 years old, are commanding pretty high rates. So even if they are replaced by newer chips every year, the older chips still hold a lot of value and can’t simply be written off to 0.

I think this is the most comprehensive look at the AI economy so far, probably a better source than the rest: https://www.exponentialview.co/p/the-state-of-the-ai-economy — it suggests everything is walking a tightrope but still sustainable for now.

> Where are you getting the 20% and 80% split?

Like I said, it's a heuristic, and the error bar on that opinion is... "50/50 split is also bad", for debt financing reasons. I'm skewing my guesstimate toward a pareto-split bear case, because 50/50 is the rosy-eyed best-ever case being proffered by parties who need the story to remain believable. I doubt anyone has a true grasp of the opaque financing as a single coherent picture.

In any case, I'm trying to reason from first principles.

A) The sheer quantum of debt financing skews the whole US economy, and that is a hard thing to skew. This means debt will keep getting repriced, higher interest rates, because risk exposure to financiers increases non-linearly when said risk becomes industry-wide.

B) Compute and power become inelastic, at the scale and rate of expansion of LLM datacenter. The become highly contested practically fixed resources. Prices will go up, and they are likely to go up faster with every marginal increase in demand.

C) Far better informed parties have been warning about severe under-quoting of liabilities for a while now. e.g. Some of the resources informing my opinion include publishing by Asad Ramzanali / Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator and Michael Burry / Cassandra Unchained. Worth reading their stuff:

After the AI Crash, by Asad Ramzanali, Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator (March 2026): https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=6476159

Michael Burry Warns: AI Infrastructure Depreciation Is Masking Billions in Costs https://nova.kapualabs.com/goog-sys_onboarding/michael-burry...

(To be clear, just because Burry was spectacularly on the money that one time about CDOs, doesn't automatically mean he is right about this, but he does have a habit of calling out bullshit as he sees it, particularly dodgy financial engineering of the kind these people are doing... Corroborated by others like Asad Ramzanali.)

Ah, maybe "heuristics" is not an accurate word here, because it usually indicates something based in observation of empirical evidence or trial and error, even if its typically unscientific, so I was curious about the inputs to the 20/80 split.

I skimmed through the "After the AI Crash" paper, and it is really not an analysis but a policy brief that mostly reiterates, and uncritically accepts, a lot of the large numbers thrown about in other media sources. There is no analysis of the demand side and cash flows and timelines involved, and spends a lot of time on the circular investment issue with any attempt to unravel it.

The exponential view analysis is much more methodical and finer-grained in its approach, and it addresses a lot of the aspects you mentioned, including prices and demand.

As for whatever Michael Burry has said, I've looked into it a bit (as an outsider, no inside knowledge) and I don't quite buy his thesis. There are indications from too many different sources that GPUs are economically valuable for much, much longer than the timeline he assumes.

A good thing to Google AI Overview would be "How many market crashes has Michael Burry predicted?", and wonder why all those other predictions didn't get the airtime this one is. I have a theory: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50421245 ;-)

Well, that is a good point. No the load isn't 100% constant but it's much more constant and they're using way more energy than a residential user so the "bulk discount" thesis still applies

For DCs doing training, their load is constant as long as training is happening. But as soon as they end a run, their load can disappear quickly. This is actually a problem, as the grid and generators are not designed to see massive amounts of load go away instantly

Several system operators are working on new guidelines about these large loads, and they're working on ways and regulations such that these loads have to ride out grid instability and not just disappear without warning

This appears to be from this weird graph on page 137 of their S-1, "Significant increase in revenue per dollar of compute". It's not really explained well and has very not only WeWork but also Enron and even DotCom ("number of eyeballs on the page") vibes.

It _could_ be the cost of running inference to respond to requests which bring in revenue, however the cost is described as "compute and infrastructure expenses", while revenue is described as "in-period revenue". I don't see these numbers matching anything else in the filing, however I do not claim to go over the entire document.

So to be perfectly honest I'd just ignore this metric completely :)

After "AI": Anticipating a post-LLM science & technology revolution

https://www.evalapply.org/posts/after-ai/index.html

I reckon it depends on how hot they run GPUs for how long. Running any chip at clock or overclocked (likely) will burn it out faster than "business as usual" workloads.

Defraying of capex also depends on how the hyperscalers scrap used hardware.

AFAIK, all hyperscaler hardware is effectively a consumable. Disks, memory, boards, chips; all the high-value pieces do not get refurbished into new computers for sale into secondary markets. The commercial and legal liability is too high---leaking their own proprietary IP as well as leaking customer IP, not to mention secrets and hardening configs and so forth.

I can't recall where I read it, but if a datacenter is modeled as a bunch of black-box hot-swappable shipping containers, then for pre-LLM workloads, per-container unit economics works only as long as a container delivers over 30% capacity. After that you got to swap it out, and send the black box into a furnace to recover them rare earth metals for the next generation of chips.

To a first approximation, high-throughput, gpu-maxxing math workloads (LLM inference) are surely harder on chips and memory, than are bread-and-butter SaaS / data lake / ETL / RDBMS workloads. Speculating further, I'd guess that the ~40% operating margin of datacenters is due to the relative compute-friendliness of non-math workloads for lack of better words.

> Running any chip at clock or overclocked (likely) will burn it out faster than "business as usual" workloads.

Could it be that they _have_ to run them like that because of the shortage of compute volume and once there are sufficient data centers, they can be run relatively cooler and thereby extending their lifespans? That doesn't bode well for NVIDIA/AMD.

> AFAIK, all hyperscaler hardware is effectively a consumable. Disks, memory, boards, chips; all the high-value pieces do not get refurbished into new computers for sale into secondary markets. The commercial and legal liability is too high---leaking their own proprietary IP as well as leaking customer IP, not to mention secrets and hardening configs and so forth.

Maybe that could be a catalyst for going for more "commodity" approach to hardware instead of highly spcialized (atleast for some sections of the hardware) so that the IP is not the hardware but the model/software and they can re-coup the costs by selling the hardware to "tier-2" providers that might emerge based on using cheaper second-hand hardware?

Interesting... Upon reflection, I feel like it's a "yes, and" proposition coming down to failure mode.

[Type A] Constant use a constant power level: Quantum world rules would dominate.

When run hot, electron tunneling will kill off individual transistors, and AFAIK that is a cascading failure mode once it takes root. A big enough failed spot, even if localised, could effectively kill a core (if not the whole chip---too many errors). A local hotspot will directly affect neighbours, and indirectly the chip as a whole because the same work is being pushed on fewer cores.

[Type B] Thermal cycled: Mechanical and electrical factors would dominate...

Microfractures / mechanical damage in weak areas of whole chips, and motherboards. In a hyperscaler server rack, if a board dies that part of the rack is dead---micro-maintenance is probably too expensive.

And speculating further, it stands to reason that Type B failures would likely cause Type A failures, and vice-versa.

That only explains why the price of those GPUs at resale is high, but it doesn't invalidate the fact that those GPUs are still very useful way past a 2 to 3 years depreciation schedule advocated by Michael Burry et al.

Older GPUs can still be used to run model inference, albeit more slowly than newer GPUs. We already see frontier labs turning this insight into an opportunity to charge a premium on token delivery speed, when models run on newer hardware. As AI becomes more widely spread throughout the economy, not all workloads will require fast inference, and there will be many use cases for previous generation hardware. The only exception is if the latest batch of specialised chips become ubiquitous very quickly, but then price of compute AND intelligence per watt will both go down dramatically, which would reduce the need for sustained high capex and opex

Yes it is a supply-side crunch (chip manufacturing), but IMHO, it is not temporary. Only two things will remove the supply constraint.

- Demand drops like a stone: raw TFLOPS / per model. This will happen if someone figures out insanely fast and power-efficient math (specifically, multiplication) for existing chip architectures, that makes it dirt-cheap to keep re-computing ever-better SOTA LLMs, as well as to on-line compute inference with ever-bigger models (scaling laws rule). These are different workloads, AFAIK.

- Moore's law re-starts, because someone figures out entirely new transistor designs that can deliver at least up to 100x per-core frequency gains over Si transistors (which would be nothing considering that Si transistor tech delivered ~1Mx gains since invention) and which can be manufactured at similar bin sizes, at similar scale (i.e. equivalent per-die yield), price-competitively (no more 10x the equivalent in SOTA Silicon compute).

I'd say that a math breakthrough might be more accessible than the transistor-manufacturing breakthrough.

> Moore's law re-starts, because someone figures out entirely new transistor designs that can deliver at least up to 100x per-core frequency gains over Si transistors (which would be nothing considering that Si transistor tech delivered ~1Mx gains since invention)

That assumes that there is no hard, physical limit on Moore's Law, which is obviously false. There is a limit, and as long as we depend on mass flow of charge through conductors, it's nowhere near quantum sizes.

Where that limit is has not yet been determined, but at this point the support structure to write transistors is the size of a house trailer, using a staggering amount of toxic chemicals (just to run the exotic lasers). So, advancements today may scale very nonlinearly in cost.

The very phrase "Moore's law restarts" acknowledges that we are no longer on-track.

Nobody cares about crypto anymore.

Neural networks in general are here to stay. Whether that is the current day frontier-model style LLM or not doesn't really matter. We've already had multiple different Deep Learning/Machine Learning architectures that have been incredibly applicable to multiple different domains.

Especially right now in the RAM-pocalpyse where it is difficult to get any machine, yes, these older GPUs are still very very useful. A guy at my company was having trouble getting compute allocated, budgeted, and approved - so eventually he went and dug up a bunch of old Volta-based GPUs, setup a local compute farm, and is getting work done. They are absolutely slower than current state-of-the-art, but they are still better than no compute at all.

I think one of the silver-linings of the current hardware high prices and shortages, is that people are going to (A) focus on software efficiency (B) not be so obsessed with having the latest and greatest hardware. Even on the consumer side, how many games ACTUALLY can utilize a RTX 5090?

Neural networks in general are here to stay. Whether that is the current day frontier-model style LLM or not doesn't really matter. We've already had multiple different Deep Learning/Machine Learning architectures that have been incredibly applicable to multiple different domains.

Especially right now in the RAM-pocalpyse where it is difficult to get any machine, yes, these older GPUs are still very very useful. A guy at my company was having trouble getting compute allocated, budgeted, and approved - so eventually he went and dug up a bunch of old Volta-based GPUs, setup a local compute farm, and is getting work done. They are absolutely slower than current state-of-the-art, but they are still better than no compute at all.

I think one of the silver-linings of the current hardware high prices and shortages, is that people are going to (A) focus on software efficiency (B) not be so obsessed with having the latest and greatest hardware. Even on the consumer side, how many games ACTUALLY can utilize a RTX 5090?

On the contrary. Anthropic states in their S-1 that they are moving to building their own compute (ie see page 139, Compute Investments):

>As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of approximately $895.4 billion. These commitments include approximately $447.5 billion expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $69.8 billion of these commitments are due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. A significant portion of this total committed spend relates to Anthropic Direct, and we expect it to represent a growing share of our compute investments over time. The flexibility from Anthropic Direct allows us to backfill the short-term compute we procure during periods of high demand with more cost-effective, long-term compute as our dedicated infrastructure comes online.

So they decide to change the way they procure compute (rent vs buy) for which they will have to raise a little shy of $1T in the next 20 years, with $70B due in the next 12 months (and $450B in the next 4 years). This adds significant risk because they have not only to execute the build-up (which they haven't done before) but also raise the funds to pay for it, all while continue to operate and grow the core business.

No horsing around here, just money math that says interest rates on debt sunk into datacenters will far outstrip the most optimistic revenue projections as of 2028-29-ish, when the bulk of the debt will come a-calling.

Also, inverse Pascal's Wager, because horse v/s motorcar is a false dichotomy... they are bound by the same laws of physics (faster horse, less shit, more noise and more smoke), merely different economic realities.

Hyperscaler bet is "Superintelligence" and/or "AGI", or we will make a God. That is a technological singularity. There will be a "before God" and "after God" world, and we will very likely never be able to understand what the AGI/Superintelligence's world looks like. (Because to understand what it is like to be a bat, you have to become the bat, but at that point your meaning of "understanding" itself changes entirely).

So I believe ten trillion dollars and a bunch of pirated books and source repos, and well pirated everything, mostly of very dubious quality and provenance, will not result in a God. I've been acting accordingly.

Actually, that happened... horseless carriage company stocks are dogwater, and have been for decades.

Indeed, the entire car business first boomed, and then has continued to exist only because oil is massively subsidized. If they suddenly started pricing in the fully-loaded cost of oil into retail prices, the cheapest way to own an all-electric (forget IC engine) would be to drive it home from the shop, park it in the driveway, and set it on fire.

Come to think of it, Happenings in Hormuz is doing some of that to everyone now.

Detroit is not the city of dreams it used to be. Hasn't been for a long time.

Datacenter subsidies will burn out faster. What will remain is industrial capacity to manufacture really _really_ fast computers, at a huge enough volume, to become "commodity android devices for the common person" --- I'm betting on that.

Massive burn: the people I disagree with have motivated reasoning.[1] Would it be cope to deny that there is a bubble because one might have invested a lot in AI?

[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50422043

> The hackernews crowd just can't emotionally handle the coming economic disruption.

The “hackernews crowd” has a lot of highly-paid SC wage workers, even venture capitalists (whatever that is about).[2] Personally though I just have a normal job and don’t want to be disrupted out of how I earn my living. Now you can go on and gloat. Gloat about how you think that I will become economically destitute. This is an open invitation.

[2] But I don’t even buy that the hackernews crowd is coping about the success of AI. Most seem to be euphoric about outsourcing their coding. Any and all LLM-technical posts get hundreds of replies by eager agent managers. While the LLM-political posts get a mix of enthusiasts and haters. It’s like the LLM-technical submissions live in an alternate dimension.

Railroads, semiconductors, plastics, networking... the utility was there for all of them, and so was the potential profit.

Everybody knew it.

But some investors don't have the patience for these "sure things" to mature into their commercial destiny and others know they can siphon off a killing by taking advantage of them as they speculate.

These bubbles aren't about potential, they're about timing.

And today's AI, for as revolutionary as it may be, is taking just as long to mature as anything in the past.

Most of the top players involved in AI right now are going to be rich. And in 20 years, the world is going to involve a lot of AI in soooo many things. But a lot of shirts are going to be lost below those top players and a lot of companies are going to fold because infrastructure, refinement, and integration take time while the FOMO speculation starts as soon as the big discovery is recognized.

> US has high energy costs, it can never be cost competitive.

A non-trivial percentage of that is artificial.

When push comes to shove and enormous profits (and anything remotely resembling national security) are at stake, the US is decent at removing artificial problems.

You've already seen a ton of that related to chips and data center build outs.

Why is solar more expensive in the US than China? Mainly tariffs. Same for batteries.

Why is nuclear more expensive in the US than South Korea? The government.

Why is SMR never going to beat conventional nuclear if you remove artificial problems? Physics. Though specialized applications will be viable with SMR.

People want to do all kinds of idiotic things which make no sense. We've had excess compute/gpu since 2010. People didn't know what do with all that excess and started bitcoin and tens of thousands of crypto, followed by NFT. The claim was crypto will solve all problems, which hasn't happened. Now, everyone moved on to AI, AI will do this, that and everything else and also take away all your white collar and creative jobs.

Even third world countries like India which can't provide basic services to their citizens, have no water, no power, no sanitation or cleanliness are giving hundreds of billions of dollars in incentives (land, power, water, tax subsidies) to hyperscalers, to create at most 2.6 jobs. Google clearing land to build India's largest data centre: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dBJPf6Pxfvs

> The UK has even higher energy costs and people seem to want to build data centers here? (Or at least they say they do - looks more like land speculation to me):

There is no meaning to what politicians and crony capitalists do. It is all lies, theft and grift.

The island where residents fight data centres for water: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WuToaVyWmL4

blocks.html_en:
Railroads had some of the same issue encountered by the dotcom bubble, and in particular dark fiber: Overcapacity.

Once railroads where demonstrated to be (extremely) profitable, people kept building them even if the existing demand was already met. The exact same thing happened with dark fiber (looking at you Enron).

AI is a bit different in the sense that the capacity can be used for research, and more importantly is not bound to a specific connection (between locations), and therefore a lot more fungible.

Not sure about canals, but while I think there are issue with current AI investments, I would not conflate them with the railroad bubble on this basis.

AI is a bit different in that unlike the rail tracks and the dark fiber the data centers arent actually going to be finished. It's much more of a stranded asset - there will be piles of chips and 1/4 finished construction projects, not usable assets.

No doubt somebody will use the assets for something but it's still wildly more wasteful than either railroads or dark fiber.

Also, (setting aside Standard Oil’s business practices), this is a common meme in oil exploration historically, and even today. Early prospectors were honestly pretty stupid, and their principal differentiation was risk tolerance.

There a lot of parallels with AI…it doesn’t take a genius to see the long-term potential, but the risk is in implementation, so it’s a mad rush to the finish line by a wide variety of less scrupulous early players. Rockefeller got his big start by sweeping up failing producers who were all capital weak, and I’m sure something similar will happen here during the inevitable bust.

I can do the hard, risky work of drilling wells / deploying AI, or I can sell you a vision of that future, today. The most dangerous technologies in terms of grifting are the ones that everyone can understand.

A large number of companies failed in the dotcom crash, but the founders did pretty well if they'd made it to an exit event. Don't forget that it was a stock market bubble imploding. The founders and early employees had already sold shares in the IPOs that put the companies on exchanges. It was the investors who bought stock that lost money.

The after effects were that it was virtually impossible to raise capital for a while afterwards, so the next round of founders struggled. But then interest rates went to practically zero and money got cheap so it was all good.
