> they're about timing.

Yes. And valuation. I think the leading frontier labs will be fine in the long-run and NVidia will be fine. Some of their investors who bought at too high of a valuation, expecting to flip it in too short a time frame will lose a chunk of their money when they have to sell for less.

The hyper-scalers in the middle are the most vulnerable. They borrowed billions at increasingly high rates to lock up GPU and power capacity. They are 'ground zero' of a lot of the 'circular money' deals. Big banks who financed hyper-scalers initially, expecting they could package that debt up and sell it on to diversify, are already struggling to find buyers for the debt, causing its value to drop, which then forces the banks to cover with more collateral, and that's how the snowball starts down the mountain.

blocks.html_en:
> Your logic is backwards.

I think we're essentially saying nearly the same thing and agree it eventually leads to a similar outcome. The difference is in part saying it in different ways and in part addressing the flow and feed backs at different points. Ultimately there are three key players in an ecosystem flow that supplies end-user demand:

[NVidia (NV)] <-> [HyperScalers (HS)] <-> [Frontier Labs (FL)]

TSMC is upstream of NV but they're diversified enough to be sheltered, and end user demand is the ultimate gating factor. Most people agree that in the long-term (10+ yr) AI compute services will be a very big viable business. What you and I understand which some don't, is that the Bubble Burst scenario doesn't require growth in AI demand to ever drop. A big crash can be triggered just by the growth rate in cash flow from AI end-user demand tapering from super-linear down to strongly linear.

Much like 2008, the lenders supplying the build-out got too speculative. The fact that 10 years from now all today's AI investments and loans will look like incredibly cheap, outstanding investments doesn't matter if over the growth rate tapers from super-linear to just linear growth for 6 months anytime over the next 12 to 48 months. That's enough to trigger the Bubble Burst spiral due to leveraged and circular investments. The risk is entirely near-term timing and relative over-valuation, not absolute value in the long-run. I think some are assuming we're saying growth or value will decrease in absolute terms. I'm certainly not. I think the growth rate in actual cash flow from AI end-user demand will not only NEVER go negative, it will continue to increase every month for the next decade - and there will still be a big crash - simply because too many speculators made leveraged financial bets which require near-term growth rates to remain consistently super-linear.

> Frontier labs are losing money and are most likely to go bankrupt and be absorded by bigger companies.

Anything's possible but I don't see how that's likely. It really depends on who is left 'holding the bag' on committed contracts and callable loans. While all the Frontier Labs have essentially taken what nets to equity-secured loans from NV, AFAICT it's not collateralized in a way that allows NV (or HS) to force FLs into bankruptcy. Creditors with capital were willing to take FL equity for cash, making them investors, not creditors. After their IPOs, that will change. FL sales will continue to steadily grow but not at rates required to make their equity worth what investors thought it would be worth in the time frame they expected/needed.

> Hyperscalers ... already control the frontier labs.

Through what legal or financial mechanisms is this control? If end-user demand continues to grow super-linearly, FLs will need more compute from HS than they get. In that case, HS will continue to have pricing power due to scarcity increasing. If future end-user demand growth rates taper from super-linear to just strong linear, FLs will need less compute than they've projected and HS pricing power will erode. This is the feed back point most likely to trigger the Burst Spiral (more specifically, watch things like the spot market for 12 month future contracts for B300 computer/hours).

Hyperscalers ... are ultimately profitable

Unlike FLs, HS are collateralized to their bankers, their GPU and their power suppliers in ways which CAN force bankruptcy. If the growth rate in demand tapers, even a little, prices will fall. HS have bought, and committed to buy, more GPUs, power and real estate sooner than they are going to need it from bankers who can force them into bankruptcy. The HS have secured their loans by pledging their GPUs, committed power contracts and real estate/physical plants as collateral.

When cash flow is high and the growth rate of cash flow keeps increasing, lenders will loan $2 to $5 for every dollar of 'sellable asset' the loan is secured by. The HS are already extending their GPU depreciation time frames to SIX years which inflates the forward book value of their GPUs - so they can borrow more at cheaper rates. When the growth rate of cash flow starts to taper from super-linear to just very good, lenders start to demand more collateral per dollar (or capital costs go up). Both are already happening. NV and FL will be damaged but HS are most likely to get screwed because NV and FL have investors (who just lose lots of money) but HS have cash creditors who can force bankruptcy and will panic when they realize they're holding billions in loans secured by evaporating collateral value - much like "Collateralized Debt Obligation (CDO)" contracts triggered the 2008 financial collapse. The irony is those tens-of-thousands of residential houses backing the 2008 CDOs were still livable homes and almost all are worth more today than they were at the peak of the bubble. No one thinks the mountains of GPUs (and future GPU deliveries) HS overpaid for will be worth more than ~50% in 3 years.

blocks.html_en:
Got it. As I mentioned, owning shares isn't "control" (absent a separate agreement), so they have no control to force anything, they can just choose to dump their shares, depressing the share price while losing money themselves.

> hyperscalers will just get drastic haircuts.

I think everyone may get drastic haircuts (though I'm still hoping for a 'soft unwind' type slow-mo crash, I don't think the odds are good). Hyperscalers are what probably breaks first and worst because more of their money is from creditors vs investors, combined with, more of their creditors are financial speculators / banks who have no vested interest in propping up the AI market (like an NV, FL do). They are only loyal to their cash.

I don't think they are talking about the ones you listed, but companies like CoreWeave.

Google, Meta, Amazon, MS have huge cash-producing businesses they can just fall back on. Of course the stocks will get hammered in the short term, but they are still sitting on cash volcanos.

Pure AI plays are what are most at risk. In the bad case, all the CoreWeave type companies have their assets acquired on the cheap by the existing big players. In the armageddon case, companies like Anthropic and OpenAI also end up in the discount bin.

> Wait... with hyper-scalers, we are talking about Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, are we not?

No, by Hyperscalers (HS) I was referring to the pure-play companies doing the massive build outs of mega-scale data center farms for FAANG and frontier labs (FL). FL / FAANG own some of their own mega-scale data centers but they don't want their business to become too invested in real-estate and GPU depreciation. While it might lower costs to invest BIG capital in vertical integration (owning the whole value chain), the margins in that part of chain are too low to support FAANG stock prices.

So they are using a mix. Some of their own but mostly leveraging OPM (other people's money) through Hyperscalers for pure-play AI. FAANG view data centers necessary for their own core product needs (like AWS or Google Search / Gemini) in a different financial bucket than pure play AI scaling. The fact they are able to resell their excess DC capacity for pure AI to OAI/Ant so profitably right now is an opportunistic windfall, not a long-term plan. In fact, it's actually off-plan in a sense because their financial plan was not to invest tons of capital to sell AI compute on "margin-plus". It's just that the "margin-plus" margin is incredibly frothy right now. Their strategists don't think that will still be true in five+ years.

That's why their long-term mode is leaning to doing a mix and largely relying of external Hyperscalers for non-core AI capacity. Their strategy is generally, "Own our own AI compute for minimal baseline needs for our branded products (we sell to the final end-user)." Then they want to use Hyperscalers for non-core and excess capacity because HS are borrowing billions on debt markets using FAANG contracts to secure those loans. I explain why and how we can be in both 'rapid growth' and 'increasing bubble danger' at the same time in more detail in my sister comment: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50430395.

blocks.html_en:
Agreed,

I believe AI is here to stay as general concept turned into practically working implementation.

What that practicality means is we all who consume AI are learning but we're still in the early adopters phase of all that.

Of course AI companies invest a lot and try to stay on top of the traction but I also believe not all of them will survive test of time.

I personally believe that a lot of over investment in data centers and supply of energy will be burnt and will have to be reinvested somewhere else when technology advances enough to "miniaturize" AI enough so it won't require couple of football fields to provide what it does today.

I do believe cloud based AI will be always attractive to small business if price is right and to big enterprises so they don't need to invest inhouse for the scale they need, but that will be sort of alliance based enterprise B2B market.

anything between (including me for the scale I represent business wise), I can't wait until I will be able to buy appliance from 12 to 48U maximum that can do all what me and my company needs AI wise as local AI.

moment subscriptions become equally expensive as pay as you go models, I switch to mac studios with 96GB and reasonable weighted models that will be specialized in something instead of one LLM/AI to prompt everything to it and hoping it can address all sort of problems as one solution.

AI one day must fly to space, be called Mother and discover aliens. it can't be 6 football fields as physics won't let it take off. It must be one day small enough so we all can have ChatGPT 6.1 medium model at home without subscription, just as fixed price with TCO over lifecycle of the whole appliance (software + hardware together)

that may become a drama to many companies that apparently may not be worth trillions unless they diversify enough its AI offering.

AI is taking just as long to mature as anything in the past, and it will take 20 years?

I don't think so.

The reality is that the adoption is incredibly fast and that revenues of the AI labs are like doubling by the quarter.

Further, there is the expectation that breakthroughs in applying AI to science, robotics, or medicine may unlock trillions in value.

That this will take 20 years, rather than happen before 2030, is just speculation. None of us can see the future.

The bubble exists because c-suite people are sheep. They follow the herd, and the frontier CEO wolf-wannabes have been trying to herd them in a profitable direction.

But herds are easily frightened, and there's always a danger they'll stampede in a different direction.

And the risk of a catastrophic AI-enhanced online blackout is increasing.

I don't assume I'm the smartest guy in the room though, so for all of our sake, I hope you're right.

> Railroads, semiconductors, plastics, networking... the utility was there for all of them, and so was the potential profit.

I don't see all these things as being comparable to AI... At the bottom, they were "100%" technologies. Trains were just able to transport commodities, and the internet was able to reliably connect computers. So their path to success was about gaining market.

Since they were 100% technologies, they disappeared. One could build solutions using them and forget they are building blocks, because they just worked.

LLM AI is different at the fundamental level, because it's non-deterministic. It needs human-in-the-loop. It won't ever disappear. Gaining market share doesn't fix anything.

blocks.html_en: Their point is (and I tend to agree), that LLM AI is not different at the fundamental level. The idea is that e.g. coding capability will be a standard feature of future computing hardware, not a very expensive service you rent. Anthropic is the current-gen mainframe operator selling time-shared access. In the future, that capability, too, will just be a commodity, i.e. a part of the silicon in your notebook or smartphone or whatever will replace those.

If SMEs were able to buy and host their own GPUs, they would not hesitate to avoid paying a subscription for access to AI tools. They're already starting to do this.

Models already are a commodity, the massive bump in access prices to profitable levels is not going to happen, because businesses will not pay it.

I agree about timing, but not the speed:

> And today's AI, for as revolutionary as it may be, is taking just as long to mature as anything in the past.

They may be as expensive to mature (in terms of equivalent duration of total economic output), but by the wall-clock we've gone from "invent Transformers to make translation less bad" to "solves Millennium maths problems" in 9 years.

After 9 years of railroads… well, those were originally an Ancient Greek way to drag ships over an otherwise annoying bit of land, and the more modern attempt had wooden rails and a rope for humans and animals to pull for around 250 years so let's say after 9 years of the steam locomotive: 1784 for the prototype, 1802 for the "first full-scale working railway steam locomotive" (according to Wikipedia), so 9 years past the invention and it was still a prototype.

Semiconductors (well, transistors, i.e. us understanding the process and doing it deliberately, rather than getting lucky with cat's whiskers before we had any clue about quantum mechanics) did at least get commercialised in less than 9 years, but AFAICT in the form of "now our radios are better, sturdier, and smaller" which is a rather smaller change than what's already happened since Transformers.

(Of course, why Transformers, rather than the other attempts at AI? Transformers are when people cared this time around, but there have been previous AI bubbles. I'd argue those are like pointing at 1515 (or the Ancient Greeks) for the railway, or cat's whiskers for semiconductors).

blocks.html_en: Semiconductors (well, transistors, i.e. us understanding the process and doing it deliberately, rather than getting lucky with cat's whiskers before we had any clue about quantum mechanics) did at least get commercialised in less than 9 years, but AFAICT in the form of "now our radios are better, sturdier, and smaller" which is a rather smaller change than what's already happened since Transformers.

blocks.html_en:
> is taking just as long to mature as anything in the past.

WHAT?!?

This is a wild statement to make.

The pace of AI development and adoption has been insanely fast compared to virtually every major technological revolution in history.

We've gone from AI barely being useful to hundreds of millions of people using it in their daily lives in just a few years.

I think the internet and social media have completely warped our perception of time if we're looking at what's happened with AI over the last 3–4 years and concluding that it's taking too long to mature.

Rough estimate from 'invention' to 'widespread adoption':

* Automobiles: 1886 invention → 1920s mass adoption. ~40 years.

* Airplanes: 1903 first flight → 1950s mass commercial air travel. ~50 years.

* Plastics: 1907 Bakelite → 1950s widespread consumer applications. ~40+ years.

* Mobile phones: 1973 first handheld prototype → 2000 majority US adoption. 27 years.

* Personal Computers: ~1975 → 2000 majority US household ownership. ~25 years.

* Smartphones: 2007 iPhone → 2013 majority US adult adoption. 6 years.

* Chat GPT: ~3 years from GPT-2 "it kinda chats with you" to GPT-6 Astra "It's writing entire code bases"

I've been saying for awhile now that the utility is increasingly undeniable. It's amazing technology and for better or worse, is transforming the tech industry (in particular). I just wish we lived in a world without the speculative bubbles, because if this had been developed slowly, deliberately, over time, there would be no necessity to cast aside troublesome details like safety, suitability, and ethics...and we could enjoy the fruits as it was implemented gradually, responsibly, as it matures. As opposed to going "wow, this is really cool, but gosh I feel shitty about using it..."

Nor would it have been thrust blindly into the hands of your manager, the marketing department, the CEO, and countless other folks who have no understanding of how it works, its limitations, or its risks.

I am also a European. Our oligarchy looks different for sure (and look into the history of pedophile scandals in Belgium, BTW).

I am not as optimistic as you. We seem to be stagnating our way into a stark choice between becoming an American tech vassal, a Chinese tech vassal, or losing out the remnants of our ability to compete on the world markets. Half of the continent borrows money at an unsustainable rate in order to pay millions of people to do nothing for decades.

We have made decisions that looked reasonable at the time they were made, but too much has changed in the meantime and now we are stuck in bad equilibria.

The Bismarckian pay-as-you-go pension system was stable as long as people had plenty of kids and died, on average, a few years after retiring. Now they have one kid and spend 20 years in retirement before they die. The maths of that system just does not work out anymore.

The European highly regulated industry was king as long as the rest of the world had no other choice, but now that Asia has industrialized, they are blowing us out of the water. First with lower prices, but now also with quality. German exports are half of what they used to be, with another halving expected. And of course without exports, our current social spending cannot be sustained either - you cannot keep such a massive redistribution mechanism running on an economy based on selling each other cups of coffee in a beach bar.

Our most talented engineers tend to move abroad and stay there. Brain drain is one of the most serious things that can happen to a country or a continent, and we are suffering from it.

We just cannot continue to live like that, something will have to yield, but many voters just don't want to hear that.

Bubbles aren't caused by betting on the technology. They're caused by betting on the wrong companies. Say you have railway, and there's 5000 railway companies. At this point no one has any idea what good looks like, and it changes every 6 months. Investors bet on all 5000, and once all the drama is over, there are 3 companies still capable of competing in the railway business. The investors in the other 4997 get screwed, but since the investors also bet on the winning companies, theres a good chance the actual successful companies themselves get screwed because their investors are broke. There is then intense consolidation, and one of the 3 to nail the technology is still left standing while somehow there are now 3-4 other companies that won by taking talent and inventions from bankrupt companies or just by peaking after the bubble burst. About 20% of the bubble companies have also survived by finding niches.

That's a bubble. It happens every time because it has to happen every time. If you stay out of the game, the people who stay in the game win and your holdings in redundant technology are worthless.

Bubbles are caused by reckless stock purchases leading to insane, unjustifiable valuations, regardless of the company's prospects.

Hysteria + widespread financially illiteracy means there are lots of people prepared to buy AI stocks at any price. They're adamant to get in (FOMO).

Suppose OpenAI will be a successful company into the long term, and you bought its stock at a $5T valuation. After several reporting seasons and subsiding hype, its true worth turns out to be closer $1T. OpenAI could still be enormously successful, but anyone you bought at much over $1T valuation is going to get hurt.

The last few bubbles only popped partially, with the governments (mostly the US, but not exclusively) moving fast to save some companies involved, at a high cost to tax-payers that immediately inflated some other bubble to take their place.

That means that in reality we didn't get any single actual bubble pop since the end of WWII. That may happen again this time, or maybe it won't. The amount of money running around is looking like something the governments can't save, but I did think the same in 2007.

Anyway, no financiers and entrepreneurs never know what to do with a black swan.

What on earth makes people assume there's still huge growth possible in the information sector? We've long been at the very end of the information age and even the latest attempts to squeeze out more benefits using "big data" have failed spectacularly. Especially when it comes to actually producing physical wealth i have seen no indications at all that we can increase anything drastically with a more efficient permutation of information. For example, Let's assume AI "solves" the traveling salesman and let's assume it indeed does find a better route for the delivery guy, what kind time savings are we looking at? The 8 hour route is done in 7.5? That's not going change any society in any measurable way. The just in time industry might become even juster in time but that's about it.

It might be dated but not too long ago a report showed the effect AI had on the SAP 500 and 490 companies couldn't even find any substantial improvement. Mind you, this is during the craze, this is happening while every manager has all the incentives to use as much of the technology as possible, lest they be the one that missed out on the new steam engine. All of these companies invested heavily in cars because none of them wanted to be stuck using horses while everyone else drives off into the sunset... yet most of them didn't manage to measurably outrun the people on horses. That's not the prediction I would have made if I were switching from horses to cars.

This reads less like a bulwark against sensationalism and more like an attempt to remain ideologically safe in what appears from many angles to be an extremely steep exponential start of what we can probably agree is an S-curve.

> And today's AI, for as revolutionary as it may be, is taking just as long to mature as anything in the past.

I suspect this opinion may come across as naive for the myriad software engineers whose job has become pressing the enter key. Your point about timing is based on solid principles, but I don't think your comment contains a satisfactory argument that the timing is incorrect.

How do you know we aren't already through the exponential part of the S-curve and about to enter the AGI winter (i.e. AGI will require a fundamentally different technology than LLMs that is still decades off)?

If no one is willing to pay increasingly high costs of training frontier models, we'll still have the models that we have now that can be fine tuned for incremental improvements. Still tons of utility in that, but little investor upside.

> How do you know we aren't already through the exponential part of the S-curve

From a recent METR report, benchmarks point towards an acceleration, LLMs are getting better at a faster rate. There's no sign that we are about to reach the top of the S curve.

> increasingly high costs of training frontier models

Somewhat surprisingly the gains do not seems to come from more compute, we have on the METR report:

> We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.

Link to said report: https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleratio...

> Somewhat surprisingly the gains do not seems to come from more compute

I think this could form part of an argument that acceleration is slowing. It's only because we are not making as much improvement out of hardware gains that we're having to find the improvements in more complex architecture and more tricky to create training data.

The fact that the gains are not coming from the traditional place gains come from in technology might be a sign that a high percentage of the low hanging fruit has now been picked.

That's not the difference. The difference is the distinction between core infra, B2B services, and B2C services.

The companies that sold core infra during dot com mostly died, because they invested in fiber etc far too quickly. Likewise with server factories like Sun.

The B2B and B2C survivors were patchy. A few did extremely well but there were a lot of casualties.

The biggest winners offered B2G - business to government - disguised as search and social media. They were actually selling individual user profiling and targeted ads, and that turned out to be the biggest money maker.

The reason Anthropic and OpenAI appear wildly overvalued is because their offering isn't AI in some abstract sense, it's the next generation of surveillance and persuasion technology. But now with corporate surveillance in addition to the traditional profiling and targeting.

You can tell a lot about what someone is doing - and the industry is doing in general - by looking at everyone's code bases. You don't need to train on them or steal keys to extract immense value.

Potentially there's also the option to eventually make claims on corporate IP developed with AI tech.

Anyone who thinks the companies who pulped and torrented whole libraries of books for their training data would never, ever, pinky promise, try to extract value from the code they're generating is being very naive.

> Railroads, semiconductors, plastics, networking... the utility was there for all of them, and so was the potential profit.

I wonder why so few people make the comparison to the recent VR hype. We heard the same things there about its unlimited potential, how it's inevitable that we will soon resolve all its shortcomings and that it will become ubiquitous.

I still believe VR will eventually live up to its potential, but no one can deny that bubble has popped after Meta took a huge loss on it. It took too long to resolve the hard problems so the timing didn't work for them.

> If anyone can trivially create, every creation is meaningless.

Everyone has always been able to trivially create. We live in an attention economy, not a creativity economy. Meaning you can create crap (or ai slop) and people will consume it if you know how to get their attention.

Attention is what gets money. Creation is just fuel for attention. Quality is a part of the equation, but much less important than people generally believe.

Here's a legacy document explaining all this since long before ai or the internet was around: https://archive.org/details/TheManualHowToHaveANumber1TheEas...

> Almost everywhere I the world railways are state owned and heavily subsidised and still aren’t that attractive to customers.

That's a remnant of the past, where only a nation state could afford massive projects such as creating a railway line crisscrossing throughout a massive country.

Since the last couple of decades we see private companies investing in railway lines, including high-speed railway corridors. We also see a major liberalization push in Europe to decouple railway operators from infrastructure maintainers, and now there are plenty of private companies operating railway services across the world. In Spain alone there are 2 or 4 private companies providing high-speed railway connections between major urban centers.

blocks.html_en:
> but highways and automobiles took over

The reasons for this are complicated and nuanced though.

Governments think they push the financial burden of transport maintenance on the people (and its a good tool to register and control people too, but thats not a strong consideration I wouldn’t wager), so they fervently cut spending on public transport and curtail cycling infrastructure in favour of cars.

But roads themselves operate at a crazy financial loss and are one of the reasons governments are in crazy debt (which nobody wants to acknowledge).

This is because road maintenance is significantly more expensive than building new roads. Which means that road use becomes heavily subsidised (much more than trains cost per user) but the cost of vehicle ownership, despite that heavy subsidy, is still enormous and one of the largest expenses an average person can have.

You have to understand that road wear is governed by the https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_power_law

"The fourth power law (also known as the fourth power rule) is a rule of thumb which states that the damage to the road caused by a motor vehicle increases in proportion to the fourth power of its axle load. This law was discovered in the course of a series of scientific experiments in the United States in the late 1950s and was decisive for the development of standard construction methods in road construction."

"Example: Car (total weight 2 tonnes, 2 axles): load per axle: 1 tonnes vs Truck (total weight 30 tonnes, 3 axles): load per axle: 10 tonnes. [...] The resulting damage differential between truck and car is 15,000 to 1"

PS: this is something electric car proponents don't talk much about

Europe is a large disparate continent, but I don’t know any country (neither Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Estonia, Finland or the UK) that covers road maintenance costs with fuel levies.

In fact in the UK you would be forced to aggregate all fuel and road tax and offset it against road maintenance because there is no direct correlation to be made, as tax is “one big bucket”.

The majority of the planet are going from one point of interest to another at a relative constant rate- but yes people are spread further and further- ironically this is helped by requiring huge parking space everywhere anyone needs to go, and needing huge houses so you can park multiple cars outside. Its a self-reinforcing problem.

(This is most evident when comparing cities like Malmö in Sweden with Orlando, FL. Malmö has a higher total population but approximately 1/20th the road surface- yet in Orlando I kept bumping into the same people everywhere I went because we’d all drive to the same Restaurants and Shops; and despite that happening we had to drive 20-25 minutes to get there! Weird coincidence or natural concentration points? Someone smarter than me would have to say).

Just to be clear, there's no specific "road tax" in the UK - it was abolished in 1937. Instead general taxation (e.g. income tax) pays for roads.

Your point about places becoming further apart has been made by Cory Doctorow who refers to it as "geometry hates cars".

Edit: found the Cory link - you might find it interesting, but I suspect it's detailing what you already know

https://thewaroncars.org/transcript-episode-79-the-end-of-ub...

The "road tax" misconception is why I feel the need to point it out as it is inaccurate and is used to weaponise hate against cyclists (e.g. "Don't bloody pay road tax"). In reality, most cyclists also drive (not me, though), but everyone who pays income tax is funding the roads which I agree with as they are shared infrastructure. However, it does mean that drivers are being subsidised by non-drivers.

Of course, with the 4th power weight relationship with road damage, ordinary cars are not really causing much damage compared to buses and trucks, so maybe it's better to state that we're subsidising logistics companies.

I can cycle anywhere in my city in 15 minutes- and anyone else can too.

Yes, it gets cold in the winter in Sweden- and I sometimes have to wear rainware. But the lack of noise, huge highways and being able to walk if necessary is such a crazy feeling of freedom that you can't possibly imagine.

I literally mean, you cannot imagine.

Being able to drink a beer, and then walk with a friend in the evening with my bike in hand, being able to park anywhere at any time, and being able to replace/fix my bike with no money (or, even buy a new bike without crazy paperwork or registration or licensing for my ability to drive it).

Not having anxiety about paying for parking, fuel or ensuring that I have a place to park, not to mention the lack of abusive road-rage folks.

I've lived in other places, and I've visited supposed "car-utopias" where everything is built to "great" standards and honestly the quality of life is just many orders of magnitude inferior. I've never been to the US and stayed in a nice quiet house without it being 30 minutes drive (in stop/start traffic and with aggressive drivers who cut you off) from anything of any value.

So, no, it's not the best option. It's the best option you can think of.

> I've never been to the US and stayed in a nice quiet house without it being 30 minutes drive from anything of any value.

I'm in Canada, not the US, so maybe it's slightly different. But where I live seems quiet. Comparable to the country at worst, where I lived on a through-road to a beach. It's a suburb but I could walk to a grocery store in like 10 minutes, if that counts as something of value.

> in stop/start traffic and with aggressive drivers who cut you off

The stop and go can be bad during rush-hour near major highways, true. But aggressive drivers sounds like a one off bad experience, or lack of experience driving. I'm not saying it doesn't happen, but they're an exception not the norm.

> So, no, it's not the best option. It's the best option you can think of.

I'd argue a general solution is better than one that only works for some people.

I wouldn't consider a 25 minute commute while being exposed to freezing rain or heatstroke weather to be the best in any way.

Before I could afford to live in the city, I had A 40 minute commute when the roads weren't closed from snow. That's basically impossible on a bike.

blocks.html_en:
To be completely fair with you, I've travelled the length and breadth of the US over the course of 15 years and a dozen trips. Bryan, Ohio- NYC- Philly- Montclaire, NJ- SF, LA, Seattle, Austin, Kissimi/Orlando, Miami and Daytona... In fact I'll be back in Orlando 3 weeks from now.

I've had, what I consider, enough experience to feel like I know what I'm talking about here.

However, I haven't been anywhere in Canada except Vancouver and Montreal (and: downtowns there exclusively) so you could be right that there's something I'm missing, though you said 25 and I said 15, and I'm going to summon that one thing I said before: it was a 40 minute commute because everything has to be made so far from everything else.

In Sweden the first snow that is cleared is the bike paths, it's quite safe- and ye, if it's not clear: It snows in Sweden.

My personal opinion is;

A) People drive to nice train stations which great parking or make use of a wide bus network (which runs infrequently to very low density neighbourhoods)

B) People cycle where they can.

C) the roads are used for deliveries, disabled people and when people need to transport their own heavy goods on the occasion it's required,

D) Minor enforcement based on ANPR (need an expensive permit if it's parked for an aggregate of 10h over a month downtown and a minor limit on how many trips can be made) To keep the roads free for those who really need it.

I know public transport gets a bad rap, but that's because the public transport system available in NA is somehow pretty scary and filled with the worst of humanity. Rubbing shoulders with people doesn't have to feel awful, it does when there is overcrowding and a separate social safety issue.

To be completely fair with you, I've travelled the length and breadth of the US over the course of 15 years and a dozen trips. Bryan, Ohio- NYC- Philly- Montclaire, NJ- SF, LA, Seattle, Austin, Kissimi/Orlando, Miami and Daytona... In fact I'll be back in Orlando 3 weeks from now.

I've had, what I consider, enough experience to feel like I know what I'm talking about here.

However, I haven't been anywhere in Canada except Vancouver and Montreal (and: downtowns there exclusively) so you could be right that there's something I'm missing, though you said 25 and I said 15, and I'm going to summon that one thing I said before: it was a 40 minute commute because everything has to be made so far from everything else.

In Sweden the first snow that is cleared is the bike paths, it's quite safe- and ye, if it's not clear: It snows in Sweden.

My personal opinion is;

A) People drive to nice train stations which great parking or make use of a wide bus network (which runs infrequently to very low density neighbourhoods)

B) People cycle where they can.

C) the roads are used for deliveries, disabled people and when people need to transport their own heavy goods on the occasion it's required,

D) Minor enforcement based on ANPR (need an expensive permit if it's parked for an aggregate of 10h over a month downtown and a minor limit on how many trips can be made) To keep the roads free for those who really need it.

I know public transport gets a bad rap, but that's because the public transport system available in NA is somehow pretty scary and filled with the worst of humanity. Rubbing shoulders with people doesn't have to feel awful, it does when there is overcrowding and a separate social safety issue.

Not even the US, the country that was the most crazed about highways and car infrastructure in the 20th century, demolished its railways - the cargo proposition is just too objectively good. Semi trucks will never have the unparalleled efficiency of strapping many hundreds of tons of cargo behind a locomotive and moving it on rails, both because of their size and because rubber on asphalt is just less efficient.

Passenger rail also makes sense because the same economies of scale can help drive the prices down, and with enough coverage you get enough freedom of movement for 95% of people, with cars and other road transit bridging the last mile. Lots of countries do this very successfully, it's just not a glamorous business.

blocks.html_en:
Timing is all that matters here.

Humans living forever is inevitable. Galactic colonization, inevitable. Over a long-enough time scale.

AI is inevitable on the same time scale, sure. But can it actually survive as a sustainable business given what is needed to keep it relevant—will people pay what it costs to support said business—not clear. Or, at least in the next five years.

The second generation AI companies will be built on different assumptions and will likely be slower-growing, and that’s when you’ll see it truly become ubiquitous. That could be a decade though.

> Humans living forever is inevitable. Galactic colonization, inevitable. Over a long-enough time scale.

I doubt that. I think we just fizzle out. The survival of the fittest instincts that made us a successful species is destroying us as we are getting more capable. Our 'leaders' are getting ever more unhinged.

And without faster than light travel there just isn't much point in galactic colonisation. If generations have to live and die in a tin can to get to some remote star, why not just live in that tin can in the first place.

Do you say that to yourself every time you stream music?

What about the labor you steal from the milkmen, butter churners, seamstresses, and elevator operators? How evil of you.

And yeah, I did it. Not you. That money would be in your bank account if you did it. But you didn't.

I personally make these things. I'm not ashamed in the least to say it, because it's true.

It's funny how I'm working around the clock using AI. Because you seem to say this isn't work. And yet I've never been so busy. So can you tell me what's going on here?

How did I manage to build so many useful things for people?

I've had over 40 million downloads of my app recently. Maybe you should think about how people value things instead of relying on your own value system. Your priors might be flawed when it comes to how the rest of society values things.

I am criticizing you, and I'm far from the only person doing so.

At some point the hype is going to die and people are going to judge your products on their actual stability functionality. So far everyone who reviews them at the very least finds them fundamentally broken, and there is no professional adoption of any significance, at least not outside of the AI sphere.

The arrogance is astounding coming from someone whose photoshop clone can't even open a photoshop file.

The logic here is so flawed it suggests to me a significant lack of financial understanding. For example:

>If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars.

Alphabet's REVENUE was $162B, not earnings! You can't use all your revenue to pay off your debts because you have to use some of your revenue to pay operating and other expenses. What's weird to me is that you don't see a lot of people making deals that seem way too good to be true but yet the total numbers are absolutely gigantic. Throw on the fact that the stranded assets will have a shelf life, it really seems terrifying. Yet everything is being priced as pretty darn risky. I think maybe there can be a big slowdown without a dramatic pop. A sort of grind down. But there's not a lot of room for error to prevent a pop so I guess it will happen? I don't know its very weird.

Also of course this is all predicated on models not making another dramatic leap. The signals out of the cutting edge labs don't really suggest they have a model that would be as dramatic of a leap as Mythos was when it came out in the hopper. Their code quality seems about as mediocre as what the publicly available models can do. The OpenAI math results are very impressive but that's ripe picking for AI. Also they keep talking about a coordinated training slowdown which is textbook antitrust so they seem to want the government to force their hands off the "spend money on R&D" button.

So I don't really know. I guess I would say purely on vibes that this doesn't feel like a bubble but the size of the build out is just so massive that there really isn't a big window for a success case.

People keep saying this about open weight models but I haven’t heard of any real companies any of my friends work at willing to switch over to them.

My company buys Claude because it’s a trusted name with a user-friendly interface and integrations with a lot of business apps.

This “open weight models will take over based on price” is analogous saying that Linux and LibreOfficr will displace Windows and Microsoft Office in the workplace because they’re drastically cheaper.

Another analogy is that people talk a lot about the resurgence of audio CDs, but if you look at sales numbers it’s about 4% of peak audio CD sales from the year 2000. Sometimes in society a trend is more that people keep saying that a trend is happening rather than a trend is really happening.

You can't just literally drop LibreOffice into an organization and have it automatically and seamlessly work.

LLMs are, definitionally, fungible. Their input is tokens. Their output is tokens. They have minor variations in chat templates and can be trained to perform better in a particular harness (like training GPT in Codex).

Do you or your friends at work use redis? Postgres? Are they hosted at "Redis Inc" and "Postgres Inc"? No, they're commodities hosted at a huge number of places.

Yes, without a question. Fable 5 and Opus 5.5 are a step-change above what we had before. On the open-weights side, GLM 5.3, DeepSeek 4.1 v1017, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next are all significantly more capable in basically any task you can give them.

You can now have a model work on a task non-stop for a day or more. This was unthinkable 12 months ago, and unstable 6 months ago.

If you are searching for evidence of capability, just look at the amount of projects, blog posts and videos on game remixes, hardware reverse engineering, new compilers and runtimes that has started coming out in the last 6 months. Slop? Sure, but this kind of slop didn't exist at this level 6 or 12 months ago.

The web of circular financing that is going on leads to higher risk. If some ventures fail, and are unable to supply compute they are obligated to, or are unable to pay for compute they are obligated to buy, this could cause a series of financial problems for other related businesses.

I also think that some businesses may find that it might not (yet) be cost effective to focus AI use on every problem.

The pushback against data centers is getting bigger too. But america at least is usually pretty industry friendly so I'm not too sure how much it'll delay planned projects. I've read the limiting factor is sometimes just finding a source of power that can consistently deliver the electricity needed for the DCs that companies want to build.

With big technological shifts like this, it's important to keep in mind that the ability to do more with less resources can pan out in two different ways: (1) Keep doing what you're already doing, and lay off the people you no longer need, or (2) Do more than you did with the same amount of resources.

The answer depends on the company, but I think many companies are still figuring out whether and how they can exercise this new capacity. We don't know where it will land yet at a societal level. It's a parameter shift, and it will take some time. Pray that you live in a place with sensible labor laws and safety nets.

> pareto frontier gap decreasing by the month between open and closed models

This isn't targeted to you! It's a pet peeve.

They actually are compatible, because the idea of replacing workers with AI in large numbers isn't compatible with the kind of economic growth these valuations are predicated on. We are not living in pre-industrial revolution times, where most people are wasting huge human effort on food growth and physical tasks, having room to move into more white collar jobs.

So, if you have massive unemployment because AI really is cheaper than labor, you'll get a massive reduction in revenue for virtually every industry, collapsing all of these valuations. Even for B2B companies, Google isn't going to be making much money selling ads to unemployed people who can't afford to buy anything.

blocks.html_en:
I absolutely disagree number of users is saturated. Fortune 500 companies, for all of their 'AI accelerating' shareholder speeches, are doing very little to actually integrate or spend on AI for the average employee. I've talked to a lot of people who work white collar jobs that could absolutely be accelerated by AI, and they just... aren't using it at all. Some of the companies make Copilot available. Some people just copy paste their tasks into the free version of chatGPT and spend a lot of time correcting the dumb model. A lot of orgs are concerned about data leakage and just have a blanket AI ban.

I recently joined a software dev team in which nobody is using any AI at all. They weren't conceptually against it, they just didn't feel the need to change their process.

There's a lot of room to grow.

The author talks about revenue growth on the basis of Anthropic's S-1 filing, but ignores the third quarter results which were posted later.

But the AI industry doesn't consist of just Anthropic.

As far as I know, Q3 for Anthropic wasn't the best because:

* OpenAI killed it with their models in Q3

* US Government ban on Anthropic models, including temp restricting Mythos/Fable

* They decided to dedicate more compute to training in Q3 instead of inference

* Opus 5 was a disappointment and Fable 5 was too expensive to inference

* They saturated all their available compute in Q3 and didn't have anymore to sell

Their growth rate has ramped up in Q4 since Opus 5.5 if OpenRouter data is a good proxy.

Do it with a group like a book club.

Hardware doesn't last forever especially in a data center, maintenance isn't free, electricity is not going to get significantly cheaper. If new hardware comes online that doesn't allow you to payback your billions in hardware, what then? The level of rigor in the article is low.

If we steel-they the point in the essay, it still doesn't matter because a bubble is setup in the economics of the system, not whether the underlying tech works and/or is profitable. It can both work, be profitable, but have been overcapitalized before the knock on effects are in-place in the rest of the economy. This is a crazy analogy, but what if 1700s earth figured out, theoretically how to build a fusion reactor that could supply all the energy needs of the whole planet. But it cost in their equivalent dollars, 1 quadrillion dollars? You can't even integrate under their money curve to scrape together that many dollars. The only economy you can make about that is in the research side to push the cost down. Then when its dialed in, you can launch that rocket AND the rest of the system has had time at many different levels to integrate AI at various levels. OpenAI dry barebacked its way into the economy and literally screwed everything up. If they really were an altruistic AI safety lab, they should have kept working on ChatGPT, but demoed it to the world including government, so we could as a planet decide where we are taking this.

It is a huge bubble, AI is over capitalized, we have no idea what the knock on effects are and really the only benefit right now is in programming, which is huge and civilization changing. But it also has massive downsides in that it has given the most powerful even longer levers to move the earth.

This is a crazy analogy, but what if 1700s earth figured out, theoretically how to build a fusion reactor that could supply all the energy needs of the whole planet. But it cost in their equivalent dollars, 1 quadrillion dollars? You can't even integrate under their money curve to scrape together that many dollars. The only economy you can make about that is in the research side to push the cost down. Then when its dialed in, you can launch that rocket AND the rest of the system has had time at many different levels to integrate AI at various levels. OpenAI dry barebacked its way into the economy and literally screwed everything up. If they really were an altruistic AI safety lab, they should have kept working on ChatGPT, but demoed it to the world including government, so we could as a planet decide where we are taking this.

> Im not convinced by the claims of infrastructure only being expensive to build initially.

The claims seem to be true.

> A typical one-gigawatt AI data center requires $38 billion in up-front capital expenditure (CapEx) and $0.9 billion in annual operating expenses (OpEx). If CapEx is annualized over each asset’s lifespan, the total cost of ownership equates to $8.5 billion per year. Servers dominate this cost at $5 billion per year, or 60% of the total. Operating costs are small by comparison: even energy, the largest OpEx category, costs only $0.6 billion per year.

I just don't think the author really has any clue.

they seem to think that debt markets are infinite. "There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise"

> The ones that have issued public debt, like Alphabet and Meta, have excellent bond ratings. If they need more capital, they won't struggle to find people to give them a loan.

Yes, and that bond rating is based on the idea that they really don't have that much debt, and have a net profit of something like 30%. If they hoover up a load of debt, the rating will plunge.

> I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances

Its exactly about finances. The market participants that are not bollocks deep in fake Private Equity valuations are worried about circular debt obligations that are off books. The SEC has been rather lenient about reporting of non-traditional obligations (hence why spaceX was allow to do what ever the fuck it did)

For example anthropic has about 450 billion in non-cancellable obligations. the S-1 puts it at 895 billion. all of that is someone's debt.

If openAI are doing the same thing, thats pretty close to 1.6trillion in debt, both for the same customers, at the time when customers are going "hmm this isn't giving us what we hoped for the price"

The debt thing is amazing since it ignores the interest on the debt and cherry picks Google's revenue from 2019 for some reason (which is then adjusted for inflation for the comparison).

If you have 20 years to pay off 5 trillion dollars, it doesn't come out to a neat 250 billion per year as that suggests there's 0% interest and no servicing cost. Servicing costs would probably be at least 3 times the stated figure, corresponding to 10% interest paid. Some of the debt may obviously carry less interest, but the financing is opaque (as the author admits to), we have seen interests rates creep across the economy and big tech has had hits to their credit ratings.

I hope the Liberal Party can find a better candidate than the author of this piece ...

That is a weird take and after that I sort of just skimmed the rest. Yes building the datacenter is a huge expense, but you need to replace the hardware to stay competitive, and it doesn't last forever. Previously companies ran three year cycles, now five seems to be the standard. If hardware prices come back down, then.... maybe, if not those refresh cycles are going to put some datacenters out of business.

Another issue is that while e.g. Anthropic and OpenAI seems to be interested in building their own datacenters, they are mostly just renting capacity. If they can shop around, then they can get the price down, but there's a base price, due to power, hardware and staff.

The author also suggest that there's still capital to raise... no there's not. Anthropic is going for an IPO, that means institutional investors, not venture capital or borrowing and Anthropic, CoreWeave and Oracle are rated as junk. That doesn't mean that they can't raise capital exactly, but it will be very expensive and the interest payments needs to be factored into the price of the products.

blocks.html_en:
They are in Nvidia warehouses. Nvidia is selling H100s and other hardware in advance to firms who do not have data centres to put them in.

Nobody is getting fired for thinking they need to buy scarce H100s in case they aren't able to get them in the future. Nobody is even getting fired for keeping their companies out of Jensen Jail — the fear that if they don't buy the whole server stack from Nvidia they might not get future GPU allocations.

There really are analysts who think Nvidia is channel-stuffing.

If the market deflates there will be a glut of very cheap compute, both in terms of data centres (though many of them will be able to offer managed model training services instead, I suspect) and in terms of unused hardware being made available for sale.

Nvidia won't lose out; everyone else is going to.

> The current-gen hardware is expected to have only 2-3 years of useful life.

Expected by whom and why?

Google hasn't retired any of its now ten-year-old TPUs, or any of the subsequent generations. Maybe TPUs are special or Google doesn't understand compute economics but either argument requires data.

If your argument is depreciation, you're confusing a tax concept (depreciation) with useful life. Yes, they're supposedly related, but in practice, the relationship is rather loose. (Residential housing depreciates in 28 years yet typically lasts 2-3x as long and 4x is not rare.) Google's V1 TPUs

sentences.en: No one seems to worry about the demand of ai.
That makes me wonder.
My neighbors for example are normal working ppl they don’t know how to open a zip file (they call me to help them with something like this) and they are in their early 40s so not that old.
Sure companies and workflows are going to become agentic but not everyone needs it or even wants it.
Then there are smarter small models like Qwen 27b running on a Mac mini and this will also continue to get better and develop further.
If the usage is easy I see ppl downloading a desktop app that’s dead simple instead of paying for ChatGPT.
I just don’t see this growth curve going for 20 years for these companies to pay off their dept

Having dealt with many family members just like this, I can tell you they certainly can use Google for search, they just don't want to. When forced to they use it fine.

If I were to guess, a lot of people, particularly older people, see computer use outside the web browser as an amateur might a chop-saw; a dangerous tool not to be used by inexperienced hands, so an AI that can also directly do the tasks for them might solve that problem (assuming it came preinstalled or someone else did that for them). Though then comes the question of whether they'd be willing to pay for it

Heck I use copilot at work and use M365 copilot chat for a lot of short things and small scripts and tools over credits in Github Copilot. At home I throw things things into copilot chat free, google AI, and more to avoid cost.

Then all the real AI work I'm using my local setup on dedicated hardware for large local models. I have usede my Copilot pr sub a few times this month to check work but it's either:

1. I ask about bugs and security fixes, glaring holes, and other checks before calling the work complete and posting a release to my persona github. 2% credit usage over 20 minutes and useful small changes. 2. I ask about information in a repo I'm using, like GUFO or Halogen-flash-next, and some key info. 35% of my monthly premium credits gone before the one chat completes.

How can 20 minutes on a whole custom project looking for bugs and issues use almost nothing, then a question about a repo eats 30%+? I don't even have budget to learn how I failed as 2 more tests and I'm burned on premium requests for the month (in minutes).

So I abuse the free options for everything I can. Draft scripts/sql/etc, stage prompts or handoff/etc files, ask questions or research something and pass on to vs code/copilot chat/etc like I run at work (with much more credits through the enterprise plan).

There is no "honest" AI though. It is always biased towards its prompt and ultimately its training data.

Compare flights? You have to assume it is objective and not tainted by corporate bias or backroom deals(aka ads and sponsored content), unless you selfhost and find an objective model.

Search Wikipedia? You have to constantly check that it is giving you straight facts instead of being constrained by its community and safety guidelines.

The problem with so many of these usecases is treating AI as a super intelligent Vulcan who is always logical and objective aka Spock, when we are better off treating it as if it is a salesman.

Demand will not stop in the next 20 years.

> AI can understand human language.

It is a bit comical how the HN crowd spent the last number of decades trying to convince the audience that a programmer's value was actually in their system thinking, not their arcane knowledge of a particular language, but now that the language barrier is removed it turns out it was just the arcane language knowledge after all...

Although I'd posit that the old school HNers were the ones actually right. From what I see in the average Joes is that, while they can communicate with AI, they don't really see how to leverage it. Granted, the younger generations grew up in a school system that tried to promote system thinking more so than in the past, so that gap will likely shrink over time.

Building the middle system that can take any model as a back end, based on cost/performance/client choices/etc, and API style present the same interface and functionality to end users is huge right now.

Local LLM usage is bouncing across major runtimes, custom runtimes and forks plus custom quants and variations of open models. llama-swap and some other tools integrate those and provide metrics but as the field expands can't keep up even with AI support.

I need to look at tailscales dashboard/etc again. I started on that when it launched but couldn't get my runtimes to go through it. I think the easiest tie in for metrics/etc is grafana + Prometheus but you need that stood up, and then a custom parsing job for each runtime based on metrics it reports and processing that data into useful dash.

I would love to see more standards here like OpenAI endpoints with metrics and information to link into. ./metrics is great but not standardized.

Not just chat but an agent.

The agent will be running 24/7 and be triggered by different things. Chat input, scheduler, actions someone executes inside the software etc.

The SEO campaign tool? You might need to fill out a lot of different things, configure stuff then execute. In the future you will start the SEO campaign tool, the agent will ask you missing information, it then fills out everything, gets a budget and runs it. It will adjust the campaign based on feedback from the SEO tools.

Kind of a workflow engine but smart, so smart that it will handle A LOT more than what an traditional workflow engine could ever do.

Eg to help with car repairs, help plan family functions (to the point someone brought twice as much food as needed to a funeral bc ChatGPT said so), etc.It is really, really easy to use, and I think triggers similar dopamine response that has cause FB so become so prevalent.I mean, yeah, there are plenty of apps where AI fucking sucks and no one will use it, but I think basic ChatGPT-type use is extremely common already

As in, "machines cost less"? Well, this general principle has always been present, as in "sucking rocks costs much less then cordon bleu", but there are "human costs" (U. Eco said for an equivalent area) involved.

Of course spending less is alluring: but you have to be able to afford spending less. Also considering that giving jobs to people who deserve it prevents other general "boomerang" social costs.

> Profits Can Grow, By A Lot

Profits are mentioned but then only revenue is discussed, Revenue != Profit. Revenue can grow yeah but experimentation/token-maxing stage is ending and price wars have started, so I'm not sure about rising profits, AI Labs won't necessary be able to capture the margin(>>China<<), it might be companies/consumers who will capture most of it, if so there is a bubble - it is in AI labs with their trillion $ valuations and they might end up in a race to the bottom, BigTech is not in a bubble for the most part, they will endure a correction and fall back on their existing business.

blocks.html_en:
The entire premise on whether it is a bubble depends on if LLMs can be more than a next token prediction machine or not. Adding reasoning agents, agent swarms, and so on to enhance the results from what is essentially just predicting the next token still means this technology at its core only predicts the next token. It is not AGI and unless something fundamental changes, it never will be. There are certainly valuable applications for this technology as we have seen in coding, math, and other sectors. But it is still not more than taking in a lot data and predicting the next token.

Meanwhile, the major tech companies first financed this build out using the cash flow from their existing revenue. Once this became more difficult to justify, they literally set up companies to keep this off their books directly, and these companies are ultimately designed to take a loss and fail. But before reaching this failure stage and defaulting on debt and obligations, they went to the criminals on Wall Street and designed a financial product structured not all that different from mortgage backed securities. Also, as the "AI" aspects of their existing businesses expand, it eats into the traditional revenue generated by their core business, which if we remember, is the original collateral being used to justify all the debt in the first place. Now these core tech companies have to win "AI", whatever that ultimately means, to not only pay the debt from the build out, but to also replace their existing collateral from their original products. Think in terms of Google Search being replaced by AI. Maybe a clean transition, maybe not. Really just depends on the technology living up to the hype. If not, the hyperscaler companies designed to take a loss a fail, will fail and with it, the circular financing will pop the very real bubble that exists.

Speaking of IPO valuations as well, it's not to say that LLMs are not a valuable technology. Just look at what they have done to computer science already. But there may be increasingly limited returns on investment if every valuable problem to be solved isn't as well defined as logical computer science problems. Without solving the hallucination problem (as a result of the next token prediction limitations), the wide application of LLMs as being sold will never happen.

I never understand the “only a next token predictor” argument. I do share the view that something fundamental about intelligence might be missing in LLMs, but I don’t see how this argument captures anything. If you can predict the exact next word Einstein is about to write, every time, you’re as intelligent as Einstein! It seems very clear that the LLM is also “thinking” about where the output is headed after this next token.

I do hear this position quite a lot though so I’d be interested to hear more about what I might be missing.

The main criticism is, imo, that these models cannot think and have no logic. This is proven time and time again. Every day something new comes out, like counting Rs or the ”drive or walk“ test etc. These are the ”fixed“ or rather band-aided on a case by case basis, but nobody seems to be able to fox the underlying problem.

Having done my master‘s thesis on Transformer LMs, I think this is a fundamental limitation of the architecture.

These models can solve math problems and then fail to count the number of problems they solved. Not being able to count to 68 is not intelligence.

blocks.html_en:
It seems you are just gatekeeping intelligence.

"Not being able to quickly reference the sum corpus of human knowledge across all fields, or contextually learn new languages in moments, or grasp the overarching architecture and modules of a million+ line codebase is not intelligence."

This would be a pretty ridiculous statement don't you think?

You are operating on a narrow, human-centric view of intelligence here for some reason... while I bet you would say an Orca is intelligent. So what drives you to place an LLM so low on the intelligence totem pole? This is clearly bias.

The fact that it is programmed is irrelevant. The fact that at it's core it is an ingestion of human data and an output of a prediction of more data doesn't declassify LLM's as intelligent. Unless you are willing to put that same lens against how humans learn. (you aren't)

Not that these distinctions are meaningful in any way, by the way, in light of raw functionalism. I am just annoyed by the clear bias.

Why would being able to quickly reference all of human knowledge be relevant at all? Intelligence is not about speed, it is about correctness, which is precisely why it's concerning that frontier models keep stumbling on things that should be piss easy to get correct.

Else by your logic the exact same model running on hardware that's half as powerful is somehow half as "intelligent"

And no, humans and other species don't learn the way that LLMs do. That's fairly obvious even if one isn't a neuroscience nerd.

blocks.html_en:
> If you can predict the exact next word Einstein is about to write, every time, you’re as intelligent as Einstein!

Einstein is not hold in such esteem because he was really could at spewing out text or formal proofs or theorems, but because he was able to invent something no-one else could. Some people say he advanced physics 100 years wuth his theories in relativity, whether it is true or not.

So even if you can predict what Albert is going to write next, you are still merely copying old Albert. They are amazing at processing large amounts of data, naturally, but creating something new and surprising we have yet to see evidence of (the solutions of the millennium problems seem to be brute-forcing a solution based on fuckton of data to me, but I am not a mathematician so I guess it is up in the air still).

Is there any evidence that you yourself are more than a 'next action predictor with a multi-modal context window'?

I don't think the nature of 'predicting the next token' is the problem. One could argue that any organism works the same way. The problem is that we've had million years of evolution to stabilize the platform such that the important parts of it work without that many hallucinations -- and even then that sometimes fails and you get failure modes like e.g. schizophrenia, where the context window gets confusing and the 'next actions' don't make that much sense anymore, seen from the outside.

An LLM never experienced evolutionary pressure the same way. There's no fundamental difference between how it was incentivized to answer correctly when asked about how many Rs there are in strawberry vs whether it is safe to leave a house through the second story window, even though for any physical organism, those two would be _very_ differently weighted during training.

It's because of the proliferation of "insight-posting" - people thinking their little insightful "aha" thoughts are unique or have any kind of value at all.

However, insight born of knowledge ignorance is worthless. I really don't care for your great insight about nuclear fusion if you're not a nuclear engineer or physicist working on nuclear fusion, because your insight is just a hypothesis in the void that is your ignorance.

Ironically TFA falls victim to the same thing. It doesn't seem like the author is an economist or an expert of corporate finance. Their assessment of whether something is a bubble or not has absolutely no value, and carries with it the arrogant implication that the hundreds of thousands of people who are actually experts at these things never had the little 2AM epiphany that they had.

It's a smaller version of the same delusion that produces crackpots.

blocks.html_en:
If that is all you have then the next chess move will be random (or whatever token is more likely in isolation), or the stock prediction will be the same.

For the chess example to work you need the current board state in the context or the move history. How an LLM performs will depend on what it has learned across the transformer layers and in the residual stream, as well as how much chess data it has been trained on. -- NN models like Leela and Stockfish have been trained on thousands/millions of games and have a game-specific state space representation.

The stock prediction example is similar, but doesn't have a consistent state space in which to make that prediction. It will need information in its context (current news articles, stock history of all stocks, etc.) in order to be able to make a prediction. Its performance will depend on whether it has been able to learn factors that make it possible to make accurate predictions.

blocks.html_en:
It's the transformer architecture (token embeddings and cross-token encoding) and residual stream (cross-transformer encoding and token differentiation) that make LLMs powerful tools.

The key question is not whether this architecture is powerful. The key question is how well these models can represent things outside of their design.

With chess for example, are they actually learning the rules and strategies of the game (like AlphaZero/AlphaGo, Leela, etc.) or are they just relying on a large corpus of chess games? For example, a lot of early game moves will have been played out and the best moves will likely be the more frequent moves in the training set. So LLMs could do well early game based on that game corpus.

blocks.html_en: The entire premise on whether computing is a bubble depends on if computers can be more than a bit-flipping machine or not. Adding operating systems, compilers, distributed clusters, and so on to enhance the results from what is essentially just flipping bits still means this technology at its core only flips bits. It is not a general-purpose machine, and unless something fundamental changes, it never will be. There are certainly valuable applications for this technology, as we have seen in ballistic tables, census tabulation, and other sectors. But it is still not more than taking in voltages and toggling transistors between 0 and 1.

blocks.html_en:
> Adding reasoning agents, agent swarms, and so on to enhance the results from what is essentially just predicting the next token still means this technology at its core only predicts the next token. It is not AGI and unless something fundamental changes, it never will be.

A lot of people have dismissed LLMs four years ago for this reason. "It cannot possibly do coding since it doesn't think, it just predicts the next token." On the other hand, Scott Alexander did say in 2019 that next token prediction is a brilliant idea and might cover a lot, including math proofs [1]. So I wouldn't say it is impossible for either 1) LLMs to be all the way to AGI or 2) LLMs to become creative enough to tell us what the AGI architecture is.

[1] https://slatestarcodex.com/2019/02/19/gpt-2-as-step-toward-g...

An economy of scale, which McDonalds surely has as GP suggested in various areas, supports durable profits. Seems like a moat to me.

Land is the classic cornered resource. Again a source of durable profits. You can’t open up a franchise restaurant on land owned by McDonalds; the profits from traffic earned in that location are not accessible to you.

CUDA is not a moat because it happens to be unique. CUDA provides a moat for NVIDIA due to the high switching costs and network effects it provides.

McDonalds to my knowledge does not have any network effects dynamics going on however they have entrenched switching cost mechanisms in the form of loyalty rewards programs.

If you think McDonalds has no moat you’re dreaming.

Can you describe how that is a moat? A structural advantage that prevents other businesses from taking their customers, or their customers from switching. For example, how does McDonalds real estate holdings make it harder for diners to choose Burger King instead?

It gives McDonalds a lot of intrinsic value. It’s definitely a core part of their business. But it doesn’t prevent people from going to Burger King.

For example, in Paris they have two restaurants on Avenue des Champs-Élysées. While there's a Burger King right around the corner (Rue de la Boétie), a lot of hungry tourists will simply not walk in front of it.

I'm not imaginative enough to see more use cases and who will pay. You can burn a lot of tokens and dollars on math proofs. Same for white hats finding vulnerabilities in all the software. Generating video.

Personal assistants dealing with your email, filling out paperwork, and booking reservations don't use a lot of tokens.

If every software developer paid $200/month, every academic paid what they pay for Matlab or Mathematica licenses, every YouTuber paid for whatever video processing, and every normal person paid a subscription comparable to their TV subscriptions and cell phone plans - does that justify the valuations?

The government pays for surveillance? Companies pay for customer service replacements and target advertisements?

It seems like there are a few small categories that use a lot of tokens, and a large category that doesn't need many at all.

Yes definitely. All together that's probably within striking distance of a trillion dollars in annual revenue. Just TV subscriptions + cell phone plans in the U.S. alone is about 400 billion (leaving aside any other country).

When the internet was just getting started, I imagine it would have sounded ludicrous to suggest that soon, practically every single software application would have some networking component.

Similarly, I think it's a good bet that in the relatively near future, pretty much all consumer software, down to piddling little phone games, will be built with the presumption of some LLM/inference layer.

One very simple reason for this is that AI could dramatically change people's expectations for UI/UX across the board. I can see a future where the expectation is to have some natural language interface at minimum, or have UI driven a great deal by inference under the hood.

In which case, applications without these features become about as appealing as command line tools to the general public.

I don’t think the question is so much of AI is a future market, it is has the capital been allocated appropriately. And no one knows. The challenge Anthropic has is they have a narrow lead on the use case that makes a lot of money today, but new models come out every month and one tiny slip or wrong decision and they are toast. There is also a reliance on the idea that two things continue to happen:

1. Revenue growth increases 2. There are more highly profitable uses cases like code.

Neither are guaranteed.

I also think the narrative that these companies are profitable on compute is erroneous. You can’t ignore the other costs and no they don’t magically go away. Anthropic can’t stop training new models now or in the foreseeable future. Gemini 4 Carbon is about to come out and is apparently competitive. Google has other revenue sources. They are in the ball game. They can wait for Anthropic to run out of money.

Even if Anthropic and OpenAI go to zero, the bubble popping still won't hurt many people like it did in other recessions.

Actually there are two different things going on here

1. model layer companies: OpenAI, Anthropic

2. hyperscalers, data centres, hardware layer

When people say the bubble will pop, they usually mean the second one.

I don't think you read the Anthropic filing. It is substantially profitable if you exclude the one type of debt which was actually equity. It so happened that Amazon lent some money to Anthropic but it was tied to the valuation of Anthropic, which became a "problem" because Anthropic's valuation grew 10x. You wouldn't call this a loss in any other circumstance.
