blocks.html_en:
It heavily depends on the definition of "profitable". I bet you that "net earnings after everything distributable to shareholders" (i.e. EPS) would be negative for the foreseable future.

But this is a bet we can settle right now: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026... , the ammended S-1 with Q3 data (that for some reason they omited from the S-1 that made big news), page 23:

  (units in Kilo-millions)

  Revenue in first 2026 9-months  33.2
  Compute and infra expenses      18.8
  Personel                         4.8
  Sales                            5.5
  Administrative expenses          5.3
  Operating loss                   1.2 (they are still losing money before ITDA)

But lets compare this with S-1 non ammended (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026...)

  Revenue in first 2026 6-months  16.3
  Compute and infra expenses       8.9
  Personel                         3.1
  Sales                            3.2
  Administrative expenses          1.7
  Operating loss                   0.7

Hmm, seems that doubling their revenue also doubles their expenses, causing double the operating loss.

First 9 months minus first half:

  Revenue in Q3                   16.9
  Compute and infra expenses       9.9
  Personel                         1.7
  Sales                            2.3
  Administrative expenses          3.6
  Operating loss                  ~0.6 (Remember, this is EBITDA)

You are lucky you didn't bet actual money.

> The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet

Unless nobody is working on miniaturisation, then this reasoning might hold true.

As seen throughout history, any sufficiently absurd tech starts largescale (refrigerators, computer, radios) and eventually become portable.

Amortising data Center cost will take a long time. Within that time, if someone figures out how to make ai run on cheaper hardware, these data center cost will Become harder to recover.

> AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research

That will just kill the industry.

The whole issue is that intelligence (as measured in AA benchmarks for example) is not linear utility

I'm heavily biased here. We are building a ChatGPT/Cowork like solution for data privacy concious enterprise customers.

This is already starting today, not in 2-3 years. Currently customers are using our solution with cloud-hosted LLMs, and for the meantime costs are acceptable, but we are also building capabilities to do organizational rollouts of local LLMs, so that the majority of tasks can be offloaded to the local machines of the employees (which are most of the time underutilized anyways). For a lot of typical office worker tasks, this works great. This also has the nice side-effect of allowing C-level to use AI locally for highly sensitive documents, without a risk of leakage.

I would expect that the cost-concious customers will push the broader market of harness providers to allow for solutions like this going forward. I am however not sure how much this will take hold on the consumer market.

I think there's just some core arguments here that you can totally reasonably disagree with

>In theory, an AI company has to be worried about their users switching over to a competitor or using an open source model instead. In practice, this isn't a major concern. For starters, the average person...

There's two things to disagree with here. First, this isn't theory, I work at a company and use AI heavily, switching model is as simple as changing a line in a json file. And would I do it? I've done it like 5 times this year. Claude was good, then openai was for a while, then there were times gemini was great for quick trivial tasks, now I'm mainly back on opus-5-5 with astra for some more complex tasks. Secondly, I'm not the average person, no, I'm the person openai and anthropic actually make money from. Sure, a consumer might be stickier, but so far they're not really making money from consumers, they're mainly doing B2B.

The core thing that bugs me is not so much that AI is going to be massively unprofitable, I think there's definitely going to be profitable companies. I just think if you're Google, the best case scenario is you're transitioning from fantastic economies of scale in a monopoly business to a business with costs roughly proportional to revenue and no moat. That is really bad for Google and it's not unreasonable to think it's motivation enough for them to try and undercut Anthropic and OpenAI until they're bankrupt.

Secondly, I'm not the average person, no, I'm the person openai and anthropic actually make money from. Sure, a consumer might be stickier, but so far they're not really making money from consumers, they're mainly doing B2B.

blocks.html_en:
Yes! Pretty much everyone I talk to says we’re at peak AI. I think the contrarian position is actually that it’s not a bubble, and not enough people are prepared for it.

There’s also this very weird thing where we just somehow never extrapolate. I keep hearing, “What has AI done so far?” or “What about X thing it fails at?” It’s such a static, backward-looking view of what AI has done. It’s like saying, “2 became 4, and 4 became 8. Sure, but I don’t see a 64.”

Follow the trend lines. These things will keep improving. The only surprise is that we keep getting surprised.

blocks.html_en: Other than the fact that we’re due for one, this one is differently shaped in that there isn’t really widespread “irrational exuberance” and constant reporting about AI fortunes. I think your general investor is quite skeptical about AI and worries about exposure in their portfolio. Sure there is plenty of irrationality happening, but there is also a lot of real growth and changes in assumptions. Like the job market is way stronger than expected for even AI-threatened sectors (not entirely and I’m sorry if this affects your circles) but like we’re really just getting started here. I don’t think AI in today’s form will be the same as this time next year and that real growth is just beginning. All of the destruction of value that PE has wrought will only serve to motivate a new generation of entrepreneurs to build fundamentally better, more nimble and customer-oriented institutions.

If it is my son's birthday, he gets to choose. He'd pick either 'pizza from a box' (with which he means New York Pizza for kids) or McDonald's. If I'd pick up a meal from the local snackbar, from a Burger King, or bake my own fries and burger it wouldn't cut it for him. Would it cut it for me? For sure! Cause I like my fries tasting like potato without much salt, not the garbage they dare to serve at a McD's or Burger King. But not for him. It isn't about me; it is about the kid, my son in this case.

Furthermore, if we were on the go, the prolific yellow 'M' can be seen from afar, after which kids yell: 'I see McD's! Daddy can we eat at McD's today?' They want the real deal, and its standardized throughout the country (which has adapted McD's to local cuisine; example: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50423291). So in short, the kids already saw the 'M' sign that day, they know it is around in the vicinity, and you won't get away going to some alternative however good, proper, healthy, or tasty it is: it isn't McD's!

> except McDonald to taste.

'[…] expect […]'

I'm Dutch and lived near the German border. The first time eating at a German McD's was about 25 years ago, and it was an experience. Because they changed the mayonnaise to German customs. In Germany, mayonnaise is sour, not sweet and the specific McD's version (which normally is yellow, and contains, I don't know, pickles?) was rather different.

As such, your 99,9% is overrated since there's even lots of local flavours and customs, but yes it is generally good enough, and if you consider intra culture, you're flat out right.

When I look at the current capacity of AI, it really feels like there's so much potential for frontier models to be used that just aren't being applied yet. Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well.

This is a strange conclusion. AFAIK in mathematics it doesn't work yet like article says: there is a problem, point agent swarm on it, and mark it done. The math results from OpenAI and Anthropic were achieved by seeding the surface of known problems and randomly trying to grow solutions; while they got some good solutions indeed, it doesn't mean current LLMs will work for arbitrary math problems.

Correct me if I am wrong on this, I am only a student of mathematics and by no means a researcher.

For the programming part, I think author already says that automated solutions require a good harness, and this is indeed correct, but in my experience building good harness is hard and agents can not do this currently without human closely guiding them. And in pre-LLM programming practice we did not need harness at all, or needed only small part of it: so, solving programming problems with LLM involves more work than without LLM, even if big part of this work can be automated.

The rest of the article seems to be a speculation mostly based on the premise that LLM can really replace human in the loop, which seems to be not the case currently.

I ain't paying 1000 USD per year (83,33 per month) for this garbage. I pay about 18 EUR per month for a Mistral subscription, and if it cost 3-4 the cost, I wouldn't pay for it.

The beauty is the open models: the margins are going to be thin on proprietary models. The only thing they got going for it, is creating artificial scarcity. But the Chinese are able to buy them from secondary markets anyway, or via Jensen Huang's girlfriend.

Even if the US proprietary models are 6 months ahead, there's going to be a time when the competition is good enough. I believe we are already well past that point.

The conclusion I've come to is that AI is still revolutionary, and the buildout is probably necessary to some degree, but it is way overestimating the demand and pricing power providers will have.

SW can use a ton of AI. Lots of other applications can't, and they don't need the super smart frontier versions either. We just don't need all that much compute to serve AI for these applications, and people won't need to pay the margins necessary to get access to that AI. SW alone is not going to be enough to pay for all the investment.

I don't buy brand loyalty either. If I can pay 1$/m for the same thing from someone as I pay OpenAI or Anthropic 10$/m for, I'll do that, which almost zero barrier to entry.

The buildout is paying stratospheric prices on the assumption they can charge that much on the other end, but if demand tapers off (or model efficiency doubles again), prices will start falling. Everyone talks about Jevon's, but I don't really see why I'd spend more on AI than I need to do the things I want. I already run out of stuff to ask it to do on a basic subscription, I hardly need more.

The crux is this: I can spend x for y results. If I spend more, I probably don't get 10x for 10y results - I probably get, say, 2y results. So on that equilibrium I just don't spend all that much more because the reward for all that extra spend is not worth it. And if models get better this tradeoff starts to look worse, since I get more of the super-effective benefits for cheaper. Now I'm spending 0.1x for y results, and spending even x for 2y might not make sense, let alone 10x for 3y.

I have not been able to workout if AI means demand for compute for most people will mean it's infinite since you can have AI to just work on many different problems and many different possible solutions in parallel. Or if for most people (developers included) once AI is good enough for most tasks people will reach a limit of things they could want to do and find some limit of compute enough and if so where would this limit be.

I am talking about average users and developers, there will always be tasks that want as much compute as possible I suppose but these will be limited and cash constrained as they where in the past, I can imagine most developers being satisfied with finite compute and not wanting any more for their AI agents and not needing any more intelligence for their LLM's so no more training apart from distilling and making models more efficent.

The thing I don't know is if where AI is basically good enough for largely all possible things people could want to do, if the lack of demand for training coupled with the satiated desire for compute will mean hardware falls massively in price as well as local AI getting better and cheaper to run. It feels as if some of these data centers are not going to find have the issue of massive over supply.

> When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations, which makes the burst obvious in hindsight. With public AI companies, we don't see that happening. Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years, but all of them have stable P/E ratios in their 20s. If the increase in their valuations were irrational (or even just in expectation of future growth as opposed to current earnings), you would expect the P/E ratios to go up. Instead, their valuations look exactly what we would expect from a healthy trillion dollar company. When the dot-com bubble happened, it was largely driven by companies that couldn't turn a profit or had P/E ratios in the hundreds. I'm not going to pretend that I'm an expert on financial bubbles, but I've never heard of a bubble where the companies involved had such a modest valuation based on their earnings, even if their earnings (and therefore their evaluations) are enormous.

My worry isn't so mcuh the large players ability to raise funding, it's the long long tail of "AI" in everything else and especially small startup companies that looks more worrying to me.

At the moment you have young grads getting $20-30 million with basically limited evaluation of their skills, all over the place. The area I am interested in is physics and engineering, and the number of Physics AI startups for where there there are not physicists or mathematicians with at least PhDs in numerical computing as founders for example looks to me like a total mess. And I keep seeing things where very clearly solvers haven't converged then getting used as training data and publicised in press releases from companies like this. I assume that most technical areas are seeing similar. This is where the dotcom bubble comparisons are most apt.

I’m not convinced that something has to be overvalued for it to be a bubble. A lot of the dotcom stocks that went bust probably could’ve taken some piece of the pie, even if small, and made a business out of it if the money hadn’t run dry. Or if they had just come along later. Turns out the internet pie is enormous and it’s still growing. And now people are much more willing to use it for payments. Even some previously bad ideas might be workable now. But investors don’t have infinite patience, and the market can spook them.

Also, great products don’t always make great money. Some companies just never figure out how to monetize and eventually go belly up. Users may not be willing to pay what you expect, and the amount they pay may not be able to pay back your debt. Not every LLM chat app is going to survive the next few years. That’s just how it is when there’s sudden growth. Our economy tends towards boom and bust cycles.

Many of these arguments make an unrealistic assumption that humans are rational economic agents.

For instance, AI can absolutely take your job while producing unmaintainable slop if non-technical managers hate working with you more (and believe me, in any large company someone up the chain of command will loathe the very concept of having to work with experts) than they hate slop (which they won't learn to hate until it collapses their company and gets them fired).

And more importantly, a revolutionary technology with unique market-breaking utility can also form a bubble if both investors that are supposed to know better and regulators that are supposed to prevent bubbles are being baited and strongarmed into taking on risks on the companies' behalf.

- Anthropic is already expected to have junk bond status; this is going to make dealing with their existing debt rough while costs likely continue to rise

Just because a technology is going to be successful in the future doesn't mean that the current beliefs are accurate of which company is going to capture the most profits from that technology.

The internet is successful and cisco is having a blast but its valuation has still been enormously wrong during the dotcom bubble. Same goes for pets.com, etc.

So in other words, maybe the valuation of some companies is totally wrong. Maybe Anthropic is not worth two trillion, or even a hundred billion, but Nvidia is worth 20 trillion. Maybe it's the other way around. Maybe the legal framework changes and the value will be captured by the major rights holders, reddit, twitter, bertelsmann, etc.

blocks.html_en:
I am increasingly open to the possibility that AI is undervalued. There have been recent applications of GPT 6.1 to the client business that genuinely threaten to fully eliminate their development team and put the business in the captain's chair again. I'm inches away from convincing them they have what it takes to prompt the robot to manage their codebase 100%. AI adoption is entirely a people problem now. It's a much better developer than me in most ways the business cares about.

Everyone keeps pricing this as a technology thing for some reason. This is more like a new kind of thermodynamic cycle than a new kind of software. The downstream applications are inevitable. We can't continue milling grain by using live animals walking in circles if we wish to remain competitive.

I think the bubble narrative is a necessity for some technology people. It now comes off as a fantasy that this will all blow over soon and we might go back to some semblance of normal. I'd argue that we've burned the proverbial ships at this point. There is no going back.

Think about how far we've come in such a short time. It's barely been one year of competent coding models. Some parts of tech/media seem only impressed by instant and globally successful results for some reason. Something this disruptive takes time. It took two fucking decades before I had a broadband internet connection. There are massive crow eating buffets that are still attended by those who missed the eventual consequences of the internet.

> When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations, which makes the burst obvious in hindsight.

I think this highlights a big issue with both sides of the "AI is/isn't a bubble" debate - the idea that there's an established pattern that economic bubbles cohere to. There really isn't, and economists haven't been able to find a consistent pattern that past bubbles have conformed too (that isn't also the case of non-bubbles). "Bubbles for Farma" is a cool paper that tries to do this[0].

Like everyone else, I have my own opinions on whether there is/isn't a current AI bubble. But we should all stay humble and try and avoid stating anything as if it's an absolute fact.

blocks.html_en: so many variables here. Do anthropic and openai as "AI" companies last longer term? If LLMs curve off in terms of what they can do, and local hardware becomes capable of running local models, seems like they won't last that long. But if they keep improving such that massive amounts of compute will always be needed beyond what can be done locally? Then sure. But then does it just become a commodity market where all the margins get stripped right down? Do they invent AI tech well beyond what LLMs are capable of at the moment? I would imagine, no matter which way it goes, hardware companies will win.

blocks.html_en:
What exactly are the author's credentials?

Some indications in the text suggest that their insights are somewhat limited.

> In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable.

Once a provider stops such investments, they stop being "frontier" which makes them unattractive immediately. These two things are tightly connected.

> If the AI industry has to pay off 5 trillion dollars over the course of 20 years, that's 250 billion dollars a year. For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019.

Revenue vs profit

> Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness

Anybody doing serious software engineering will wholeheartedly disagree.

> People can theoretically switch from model to model, but people tend to settle in with a product and develop brand loyalty. For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used

LLMs are just one piece of the tool chain, a mostly interchangeable one. Which one a concrete product uses is not of concern to the end user. This quote very much misses the role of LLMs and their providers in the big tech picture.

> In 2023, a memo from Google called "We Have No Moat, And Neither Does OpenAI" was leaked, which outlined how the open source community was keeping pace with AI labs

Labs releasing the weights to their models is not what is typically called the "open source community".

I could go on but it's just not a very well-argued opinion piece. Unclear how it made it to the HN front page.

blocks.html_en:
> As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be.

I call this “SchadenFraud”: reveling in and playing up every little negative thing that happens in the AI world to make it look like it’s all just hype or completely irrational and will come crashing down any moment now.

There are enough people aggrieved by GenAI -- traditional media, creators, artists, coders, Mathematicians, and the list is fast growing fast -- that this kind of narrative will have an audience for quite a while.

They're not looking for solutions, they're just looking for rageviews. Worse, it gives folks the hope that things have not irrevocably changed and will go back to normal after the bubble pops.

Me, I’d rather get a stark but realistic picture of what’s happening now so I can prepare better for the future.

I'm actually convinced that an AI Bubble doesn't matter at all.

The quality of models like Opus 5.5 are already here, smaller labs can mimick these with a little bit of a delay.

Alone the current status has massive impact.

The status quo will get just faster and cheaper.

Then we have labs like Deepmind, companies like Google and then countries fighting over it (US America vs. China). At this point its not just private VC investing in it, its also countries aka military budgets or Research Budgets.

In parallel universities are doing their research anyway and if an AI bubble would burst tomorrow, Open Source and community driven would finally have a little bit of time to coordinate.

There was just last week an article about open post-training data. I think we want this but as long as frontier is as fast as it is, its not fun to play catch up with a moving target.

>The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

First mistake. No. Data centers are depreciating. And they're one or two hardware changes away from having most of the hardware in them worthless (because even if you're contend to keep running those, your competitors would move to the next tech).

>For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used. This partially offsets the risk of losing customers to a different product.

Never helped browser vendors maintain their base. Not even social networks, where the graph serves as an incentive to stay. And there's also generational churn. Facebook is a boomer wasteland now, for example.

Well, first of all, these are not one off purchases. GPUs do break and newer generations come out rendering the old GPUs outdated. I don't know if the 2.08 figure is very valid. This is based on costs of leasing GPUs from companies that may not be making money on the lease deal. What I do know is that Anthropic weren't profitable in Q3 and I'm hearing rumblings they are losing even more money in Q4.

Also Popeyes never had over $800 billion in uncancellable compute agreements. And I'm glad you're having fun with GPT, but I've moved all my projects to use DeepSeek 4.1 Flash. There are plenty of different providers. And as I use OpenRouter the change is one line.

The reason I think the PE ratios are lower than previous bubbles are because everyone already knows its a bubble. Also all these tech companies already have massive businesses and AI is not going to change that.

blocks.html_en:
>There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. [would -> should]

There is no logical contradiction even, just another race to the bottom, drying out of markets. The good ol' disruption playbook, like Amazon shrank or destroyed the markets to capture them, only now they are targeting all white collar jobs.

The conclusion starts: >I didn't write this article as some big takedown of the AI bubble theory. Even with this evidence, there are serious risks to the financial sustainability of the AI industry.

But the presented "evidence" is largely only: I don't know, nobody can tell the future. I mean there are also good reasons to be skeptic of skeptics like Ed Zitron, but Idk "modest valuation" seems like a big stretch. Also, I'd challenge the notion, that you'd only ever have to build that data centers _once_. Especially with the AI pace the chips are said to be replaced every three years, while the building itself could last 25 yrs. So even, if the run at the frontier cools down, I don't think running your data centers and models would come for free.

blocks.html_en:
> Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well.

We can START discussing this when someone defines "worse" and we all agree on it. For SW engineering, we've been trying to define "good" for decades and we still don't know shit.

> There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for.

No, that's a total straw man. For example, I am afraid of how AI will change the world, but for that it doesn't have to stop producing slop. I'm afraid of how the slop is CURRENTLY changing the world, people and societies. Frankly, I don't even care whether someone ever pays for the slop. This isn't a "I'm going to lose my job" kind of fear, it's a "we're running education into the ground and rapidly transforming into a low-trust society" kind of fear.

blocks.html_en:
"If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now."

-------------

If everyone, or even the majority, believed that there is a bubble that's going to pop with near certainty, that would tank stock prices immediately. Why would anyone hold a stock they know is going to go down precipitously? If the majority of people know it's a bubble, the bubble immediately pops. AI stocks still have worth, so most people believe there is no bubble or that prices will go up before going down.

People talk about bubbles. They worry about bubbles. For the most part, though, they go on investing as though there isn't going to be a bubble. Every bubble looked like a solid investment to most people right up until it burst, or it wouldn't have been a bubble.

So, no, most people do not think AI is a bubble. That doesn't necessarily it's not though.

>Anthropic's S-1 filing says that they make $2.08 for every $1 of compute. In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable.

If you ignore the cost of building cars, they are also very profitable.

>Profits Can Grow, By A Lot

They can also decline by a lot, and Anthropic's S-1 suggest that is what is happening, as their losses are widening, not narrowing.

>Google Has No Moat, But Neither Does McDonald's

That's why no one is sinking several trillion dollars into a new fast food chain.

>Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years, but all of them have stable P/E ratios in their 20s.

The "E" in their PE ratios is circular revenue that is ultimately derived from debt and equity, not real end-user demand from profitable companies. For some of these bubble companies, if you subtract the debt-fueled private stimulus money, their actual PE ratios skyrocket.

I could only find these numbers in articles on something called crypto briefing dot com, not sure how the author got this number from the S-1.

When using traditional business metrics, such as operational net income, we'll see that Anthropic has been in the red for the entirety of its history, at times to the tune of $3B per quarter, except in Q2 2026.

When looking at amended S-1 (with Q3 numbers), page 23, "Consolidated Statements of Operational Data", we can see that for 2026 YTD (Q1 - Q3) net loss was $103B; operating loss was $1,260B.

Anthropic also disclosed up to $895B (multiyear) commitments for infrastructure build-up.

Basically, the company's financial results do not allow for any reasonable valuation (which would be more than 0), leave alone $2T or even $1T. If this is not an indication of a bubble I don't know what is.

blocks.html_en: While this is true, most of Anthropic's expenses involve locking up compute for the future. But they have no idea how much compute they will actually need in the future, or how much they're going to be able to charge their customers for it. Per token prices are dropping like a rock, and performance optimizations are making model serving more efficient. Combine that with the comparatively slower growth in organic AI demand (compared to debt-driven/investor subsidized demand), and you have the very real possibility of a 2000-style "dark fiber" problem.

It's almost as if they know something about the finances that the rest of us don't...

What a weird thing to say: a business is profitable if we ignore a key part of its cost base. That’s true of any business, you know. Even if they make a 100% coverage of every request served, it’s still a far cry from the usual internet business model where responding to a request is almost free and most of the expense is the initial investment in software and its upkeep. This is why Alphabet used to be flush with cash and we get free services.

The trouble with Anthropic and OpenAI is, that not only do they need to get operationally profitable, they also need to be sufficiently profitable to provide a return on capital on all the money they have burned to date. Much of which has gone (and keeps going) not to assets but to expenses like the electricity bill. Thus, once the models are efficient enough to be served profitably, a relatively small amount of assets needs to be generating income for a relatively large amount of capital. It is my understanding, that currently the efficiency of the models does not grow even fast enough to outpace the need for new capital.

One more thing, that gets conveniently ignored when talking about AI cost is the cost of training the models. From one hand, there’s but a few institutions capable of building them and, from the other, it’s like the models grow on trees. Yes, you could run your open-weight model on your own hardware and pretend it’s profitable because you don’t have a comprehensive costing model and the infrastructure costs from security to electricity to risk are mixed in with your general cost base. But someone has spent astronomical amounts of money training that model you run and would probably like to get it back with some interest. Let’s hope that return is just money and not, say, the ability of a certain country to control the global software development process.

> Google Has No Moat, But Neither Does McDonald's

Sounds like a valid argument until you realise McDonald's is a real estate business.

There are many problems with this article. I think the bubble is real and at some point the investor money will fall off a cliff.

The value is there but the cash burn rate is extreme to say the least; and the moat is only in what you haven't released yet.

I think one of the things that people analysing the finances of the AI sector often miss is that the capital expenses associated with data centre buildout involve spending a lot of money on compute hardware which depreciates and becomes obsolete very fast.

Large companies have often changed the depreciation schedule for server hardware to 6 years rather than 3. I think it remains to be seen if this is justified as it’s not as though the pace of change in hardware has slowed down by 50% arbitrarily.

I think it’s pretty obvious to me that a data centre full of ampere GPUs is worth less than a data centre full of Blackwell GPUs. I suspect this is also why AI companies prefer to talk in terms of gigawatts of compute, as if efficiency per watt does not exist.

Data centre costs are not one-off. Some are, for buying land and building buildings and infrastructure. The actual compute however is a constant investment. I’m not familiar enough with the market to know what proportion of expenses are ongoing but I bet it’s higher than people think.

His analysis fails to consider trend lines in inference costs. A couple of years ago inference required a supercomputing cluster. Today, you can run quantized frontier tier models on video cards with a $1600 MSRP. At current trends we'll be running frontier models on a typical gaming computer setup in a couple of years. That is going to destroy centralization possibilities.

It also fails to consider the impact of 'good enough.' A lot of the build-out right now is in anticipation of trying to push the frontier level. But there comes a time, a time we're already arguably past, where models being used for a specific task will already be able to complete that task efficiently. Going way beyond the present should enable LLMs to solve ever more esoteric problems, but in economic terms if a company's goal is to harvest corn, and your corn harvester works well enough, they're not going to care whether or not that corn harvester can also solve Fugazi's 7th Great Conjecture in exomathematics.

Going way beyond the present should enable LLMs to solve ever more esoteric problems, but in economic terms if a company's goal is to harvest corn, and your corn harvester works well enough, they're not going to care whether or not that corn harvester can also solve Fugazi's 7th Great Conjecture in exomathematics.

Going in reverse:

"The AI Industry Doesn't Look Like Any Bubble We've Seen Before" - It looks exactly like the two railroad bubbles. Potential profit is there, in the future. But you have to invest in the infrastructure first. If you can't make a profit and pay back the loans fast enough, the infrastructure goes bye-bye, along with all the funds used to finance it.

"There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise" - IPO is not how you raise a trillion dollars. A million, sure. A billion, maybe? But a trillion puts retail investors - mom and pop - at risk. IPO is not how you raise funds for a railroad.

"Once AI companies become profitable" - there's the big red flag. This isn't Uber or Lyft that can float along on tens of millions in corporate hand-outs every quarter. They need 100x that much money, and nobody has it to hand out. So you can't wait around for profits. There's no magic cushion to float on.

"For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever" - They will in 4 years. "normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something" - What hassle? You download a program with a fancy GUI and run it. There are a half dozen of these projects already, that provide ChatGPT on your computer from one binary. All you need is a GPU.

"Profits Can Grow, By A Lot" - Only if they remain cheaper than local hardware or open-weight inference providers. Which won't happen because they owe more money than they can make.

The sign of the bubble is all the investment made not based on stable returns, but on hype. The weird geniuses from San Francisco said the future will depend on this one technology, all work will be changed forever, and only their company can deliver it. If you don't get in now, you'll miss out on a fortune! That hype just doesn't work out. And the proof is here: the superhuman machine sucks at writing, the documents it creates are lies, and we seem to be spending more on it than we get out of it. Because it's not magic. It's just a machine.

That's just not true. Profit is there now. If the hyperscalers stopped building new infra tomorrow, they would just roll in the profits available from what exists today!

Totally unlike the railroad bubbles which built out years and years ahead with no customers and then collapsed.

> "There's Still Plenty Of Capital To Raise" - IPO is not how you raise a trillion dollars. A million, sure. A billion, maybe? But a trillion puts retail investors - mom and pop - at risk. IPO is not how you raise funds for a railroad.

You're totally confused about what an IPO is. You're confusing the valuation of Anthropic with what they will raise. They intend to offer about $100B in stock, their valuation is at 1T.

> "Once AI companies become profitable" - there's the big red flag. This isn't Uber or Lyft that can float along on tens of millions in corporate hand-outs every quarter. They need 100x that much money, and nobody has it to hand out. So you can't wait around for profits. There's no magic cushion to float on.

Most AI companies are profitable aside from expenditures to build new infrastructure to reap more profits. That's a very healthy sign.

> "For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever" - They will in 4 years. "normal users don't want to have to deal with the hassle or expense of setting up something" - What hassle? You download a program with a fancy GUI and run it. There are a half dozen of these projects already, that provide ChatGPT on your computer from one binary. All you need is a GPU.

Uhuh. A GPU. In your phone? In your laptop? The average laptop in the US is sold for about $700, desktop for about $1k. A good GPU to run a reasonable model is $10k+. It makes zero financial sense for most people to run their own inference. The issue isn't, and never was, the software, it's the hardware. And one thing we've seen from the past years of growth is that people don't look at the models from 3 years ago and say "Oh well, that's good enough, at least I can run it slowly on my $5k+ desktop". Until that happens this is a fantasy.

> If the hyperscalers stopped building new infra tomorrow, they would just roll in the profits available from what exists today!

They owe hundreds of billions in loans on datacenters that aren't built yet and don't currently have capacity for the new users and additional tokens they promise are coming. If they don't build capacity the increase of demand would cause more outages and higher prices which would crater both their use and valuation. They have to grow or die.

> They intend to offer about $100B in stock, their valuation is at 1T

That's one company, the aggregate debt of the US AI industry approaches 1T.

> Most AI companies are profitable aside from expenditures to build new infrastructure

Which they have to complete to make the profit they promised which they need to pay off the loans they already have.

> A good GPU to run a reasonable model is $10k+

Today. Due to supply and demand. Funny thing, supply and demand. It's very reliable. High demand makes supply short for a while, but then causes supply to go up. When supply goes up, eventually demand goes down, which brings prices down. The chip factories and economies of scale that will be complete in a few years will send prices crashing, as they have before. Which might bankrupt the remaining chip companies.

"Reasonable model" isn't a thing. Many different models of different size have capacity to do many tasks. I have a laptop from 3 years ago that runs local AI models. My phone from 5 years ago runs local AI models. And any strong CPU can run models (no GPU needed). Speech to text, image/video generation, image classification, research, analysis, computer use, troubleshooting, etc, all works on tiny models. I think you don't understand the tech here. Remember that many people spend a grand every year just for a newer iPhone/Samsung. They'll spend the same for one with better AI and more RAM.

You've been saying so many incorrect things.

> They owe hundreds of billions in loans on datacenters that aren't built yet

Covered by their current revenue plus 10-20B.

> to make the profit they promised which they need to pay off the loans they already have.

No, they don't need to make profit for this. Their loans and infrastructure expenses are mostly covered by a small increase in revenue

All signs point to demand increasing to match. Economies of scale let you better capitalize on existing demand, so the companies stand to profit even as prices decrease.

> They have to grow or die.

This is the story of every startup. Even large companies are subject to this in the stock market.

If you remove that sabotaging clause, you can “have it both ways”: Ai is gonna change the world, it’s gonna be slop, and you’ll have to pay for slop while grumbling that things used to better.

This article is just kind of a mess. Yeah, if you ignore all the problems, the problems go away.

Anthropic is probably the worst company to look at because they lease all their datacenter space. They don't carry the debt, they don't play the games with depreciation, and they're probably most likely to survive because of that. Detailed analysis of Anthropic's S-1 in isolation tells you almost nothing about the problematic areas of the AI sector.

And there are a few really comical statements that render this whole thing unserious:

> The reason why AI companies are spending so much money is to rollout data centres to run the AI in the first place. These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses. Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

Okay, shares of NVDA just crashed to a round-off error close to zero.

There are other reasons why that statement is not accurate, but clearly the author hasn't even bothered to think through their argument at all.

> In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research. This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.

- AI companies are limited in their ability to jack up prices by open models being good enough and inference being cheap enough that they don't have a lot of price flexibility. If you tried to squeeze $20/mo ChatGPT subscriptions up to $200/mo then customers would disappear to other providers.

- And if you instantly switch off model building, 90% of the demand for datacenters evaporates, NVDA collapses, the Neoclouds crater to zero and go bankrupt -- AND THIS IS THE AI BUBBLE COLLAPSING.

These expenses are one-off purchases, not regular operating expenses.

Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.Okay, shares of NVDA just crashed to a round-off error close to zero.There are other reasons why that statement is not accurate, but clearly the author hasn't even bothered to think through their argument at all.> In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research.

This can be implemented instantly, whereas other kinds of expenses like leases and spending commitments are a lot harder to cut.- AI companies are limited in their ability to jack up prices by open models being good enough and inference being cheap enough that they don't have a lot of price flexibility.

I think this is correct except that it ignores the hidden bubble in the SPVs: a lot of the firms who look only partially at risk have simply moved debt off their balance sheets- but to whom? Pension funds, sovereign wealth funds etc.

And “OpenAI bubble” alone has one massive implication: the likely demise of Oracle, a blue chip business that is deeply embedded into the western world.

On the one hand, if the air is let out of the bubble before those SPVs get themselves too deep into building things that won’t be needed, that is good. But nevertheless the failures of the SPVs will harm people who are not in the exclusive billionaire club.

Also there is a considerable money-go-round; the money for everything will dry up fast when the cloud LLM businesses can’t convince people to give them money to buy Nvidia GPUs anymore l

Like others have said, it is not that AI/LLMs//ML is not perfectly valid technology, it is a auestion of whether the current investment into it is justifiable relative to the demand and profit. We still buy and sell tulips y’know.

> Outside of generative AI, self-driving cars are becoming a reality, with some evidence to suggest that they're even better than human drivers.

Haven’t they have been just around the corner for 10 years now? And the problem is not technology as such, but the fact you are inventing trains that use roadnetwork hardly large enough for cars?

> AI adoption takes time, but there's no reason to think that AI usage isn't going to massively skyrocket, even if AI doesn't get any better than it is today (and it certainly will get better). In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from.

[Emphasis mine]. This might a good example of a person writing and thinking with an LLM and letting the model enchant you with its sycophantic bullshit. We might speculate endlessly about AI or any technology, but none of that is a basis on which you should throw money at, especially not as a retail investor. We can see value production of AI in software development, but the productivity increase promised is either not in the data, or it is too early to say yet. So the real valuation of AI is really difficult say still, a lot of things needs to happen, before it can be seen to produce concrete value increase. People need to stop really really fucking hating it for one.

It kinda pointless to talk whether there is a bubble or when it will pop if there is. It might happen today at market open or never. Timing it is a fools errand. Also it is kinda pointless to shout into the void how much you love/hate AI. Better use of time would be to develop the different systems and applications that will produce value for somebody. It all sounds too similar to crypto to me still…

This is a remarkably weak article to be getting as much attention as it is. It would be easy and boring to shred the whole thing systematically, so here's one example:

> When a bubble happens, it's usually preceded by the companies involved reaching obviously inflated evaluations [...] Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are all AI companies that [aren't that]

Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA are not AI companies, and [I don't really need to explain this, right?] ignoring the inflated elephant here is a hell of a thing.

Honestly, criticising this is beneath me (sorry) and I don't really want to be here, doing that. Oh, but the irony. This article ("I'm not convinced the AI bubble exists") -- this copium -- being a busy front page submission today is such a neat way to demonstrate the bubble's existence. Truly, a thing of beauty.

blocks.html_en:
>A potential way that this could be a bubble is if AI proves to be a fad. A lot of this rise in valuations has been because of increased demand for GPUs and data centre utilization, which is downstream of the demand for AI. We might imagine that the AI labs are propped up by an enormous amount of invested capital, and this capital ends up propping up the valuations for companies that make or rent out GPUs. However, this doesn't seem to be happening. Alphabet has a full-stack AI supply chain, where they create ASICs for AI, train their own AI, integrate AI into their products, and rent out compute to customers. Their prospectus helpfully divides their revenue streams into Google Cloud for their rented compute and Google Services, which makes it easy to tell if Alphabet's increased earnings are mostly because of their data centres. The answer is no. Google Cloud revenue is growing more in terms of percentage, but Google Services is growing far more in absolute terms. Specifically, Google Services revenue grew by 37.8 billion dollars for a 12% increase, while Google Cloud revenue grew by 15.5 billion dollars for a 36% increase. Alphabet is definitely benefiting from renting out their data centres, but it's not the main reason why their earnings have skyrocketed. Meta doesn't rent out their data centres at all, but their prospectus also records them having massive increases in their revenue, on the order of an extra 30 billion dollars from 2024 to 2025, and another extra 30 billion from 2023 to 2024. This isn't foolhardy investors throwing money at any company that makes AI, this is real profit from companies that have found ways to monetize AI. Anthropic also seems to be experiencing an exponential growth in their revenue as well, based on their S-1 filing. The only real unknown is OpenAI, which purchases an enormous amount of compute from other companies. It's possible that their finances are terrible, but even if they go under, I'm not convinced that this amounts to a bubble bursting. If anything, it seems more likely that their competitors will just consolidate and fight for more of a market share instead of the collapse triggering a chain reaction that takes the industry down with it.

The first reason I became suspicious of the AI bubble is it is all the same people hyping it up. The grift just switched to the new thing.

A part of the bubble that people don’t talk about are all the small AI products and integrations that don’t do much of anything. But they took VC money to build an AI project management program and now they have to cram it in there even though it is useless and actively costs them more money. There is going to be a lot of pull back at some point with these pointless integrations and I think that is going to be felt on total AI usage.

The discussion of the “AI bubble” often conflates two different things: (1) is AI going to justify the valuations we are seeing? and (2) are the specific AI companies we have going to justify their own valuations.

The rapid progress of multiple closed frontier models, along with the rapid progress of open models, suggests that LLMs will be like electric motors, not like social media. Are electric motors worth a huge amount of money economically? Sure. But none of the companies who invented electric motors are especially valuable today, because the technology became a commodity.

> There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for.

One thing to keep in mind when you're "debating" things online is you're actually debating with a tag team of people, with a whole spectrum of views. And at any point people with stronger arguments (starting from different precepts) will reply while people with weaker arguments will fall silent.

That's why "the average hacker news poster" is simultaneously rich and poor, powerful and powerless.

> If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now.

You complain that people take the bubble as a given. Yet you continue by doing what a lot of people on the other side do:

> Most (or maybe even all) programmers and mathematicians are worse at their respective field than an AI swarm equipped with a good harness, and a good deal more expensive as well.

This isn't established. Like, at all. There's serious doubts as to whether AI-driven codebases remain maintainable, understandable and trustworthy over time. You look at a snapshot and conclude, while riding the hype wave.

I feel the projected value of both OpenAI and Anthropic requires that nothing changes in a space of technology where things seems to change a lot and reasonably suddenly.

blocks.html_en:
> Is Anthropic worth 1.2 trillion when it’s not clear they will have positive cash flow in the foreseeable future?

Maybe think of it as a bimodal thing. I can easily imagine a future in which Anthropic builds a sustainable profit model, grows into new sectors, and is credibly worth 7T in ten years.

I can also easily imagine a future in which AI capabilities continue to increase but the amount that enterprises are willing to spend on Anthropic’s services to do, and in which that, plus ever-increasing competition, cause Anthropic’s revenue to grow slowly, stall, or even contract. And that Anthropic would be unable to raise sufficient capital to make up for it and would therefore forced to default on their obligations. (Or that they would be able to raise enough capital but on poor enough terms that existing investors take substantial losses as a result.)

blocks.html_en:
A fair critique. Even I, someone who started as a (righteous) angry doomer over it, have come around for the most part.

My viewpoint also shifted around the shape of the bubble. The technology isn't going away, obviously, but the valuations of these companies like OpenAI and Anthropic feels divorced from reality. Inference continues to go down, most folks don't need frontier models for common tasks (including coding), and local models provide a competitive edge in several domains the frontier labs cannot (namely value and privacy). Combined with demand still largely subsidized and the companies being deeply unprofitable, and I just don't see the investments in Anthropic or OpenAI or the sort actually paying off. That is the bubble I'm concerned about, not the tech itself.

...now when the debts get written off and all this compute is just sitting around idle, available for bottom-dollar prices to try and eke out any sort of ROI for whichever creditor(s) inherit the assets? That's going to be pretty cool times.

blocks.html_en:
>In other words, once you ignore the cost of building infrastructure, AI is very profitable.

Its not clear that the infrastructure will ever be paid back. Its also not clear that once models are trained and distilled that the infrastructure will be useful. Ignoring 1.9 trillion dollars of debt is probably not the greatest financial analysis.

>However, there's no reason for why this level of spending has to be maintained in the first place.

Exactly. So Anthropic and OpenAI might be holding the bags for latecomers who distill their models and get ahead. Sort of the Commodore64 and Atari of the AI space.

>Once all the data centres are built, AI spending is going to plummet.

Well data centers need maintenance, and GPUs and similar do have a very short lifespan. But even if spending plummets repayments on existing debt needs to be accounted for.

>In a pinch, AI companies can also cut costs by no longer allowing people to use their products for free and temporarily suspending expensive AI research.

Research keeps them in the headlines, see above about the latecomers.

>For context, Alphabet (parent company of Google and Youtube) reported earning almost 162 billion dollars of revenue just in 2019. Adjusted for inflation, that's an even more impressive 213 billion dollars.

Yep, so all Open AI or Anthropic need to do is get acquired by a much more profitable business to pay back their debt.

>at some point, the rate of increase has to level off, but that doesn't have to happen anytime soon.

The rate of increase of revenue in the AI sector also doesnt need to be apportioned to OpenAI or Anthropic. If it wasnt for their generous loss leading subscriptions or their rnd, theres not much there to hold on to people.

>it's hard for me to see AI consumption not being 10x what it is now.

Right AI consumption will increase very likely. But will it increase at the cost of an already subsidised subscription, or increase the use of cheap Deepseek 4.1 tokens.

>For starters, the average person isn't going to use a locally hosted model, ever.

Isnt this expressly where Apple Intelligence is heading? Building small low cost models that run on Apple hardware? If I was nVidia I would have both plans being run down at the same time, looking towards selling GPUs to hyperscalers on one side, and working with OEMs to deploy AI coprocessors in laptops on the other side.

>For example, I pretty much only use ChatGPT, not because I have any really reason to, but because it was the first LLM that I ever used.

N = 1. OpenAI is already what halfway to their trust thermocline anyway?

>A potential way for a bubble to pop is for the companies involved to run out of capital to spend while they grow, causing them to fail.

Isnt Anthropic already down to BB+?

> NVIDIA are all AI companies that have seen their market capitalization explode over the past few years

NVIDIA is a hardware company that can has so much demand on their products they will likely survive 3 AI market collapses.

>Alphabet, Meta, and NVIDIA

Alphabet, Meta and NVidia all have other sources of revenue. They are companies building AI, not AI companies.

>When the dot-com bubble happened, it was largely driven by companies that couldn't turn a profit or had P/E ratios in the hundreds.

Anthropic and OpenAI dont have "E" (as in earnings)

Anthropics Debt to Equity is 363%.

>A potential way that this could be a bubble is if AI proves to be a fad.

A potential way this could be a bubble is if the makers of consumer devices point customers at cheaper or local models as part of their onboarding experience. OpenAI and Anthropic get thoroughly zuckerberged by the people holding the primary relationship with the customer base.

Or perhaps, the funding to the top 1% of token purchasers also turns out to be loans, and that dries up too.

https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/ope...

>As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances.

The people bringing it up every 10 seconds are doing it to spread FUD about AI. That doesnt really change the financial picture.

Long time artificial intelligence engineer and founder here: Welcome to the feast or famine world of AI, none of this is new. This is just how life works as somebody trying to build AI as their focus.

I don’t know a single artificial intelligence researcher working in the field for more than 20 years, who hasn’t gotten laid off once or twice in their career because all of the funding fell out for whatever their AI project.

Not only that it was usually funded by some government, and so you had to deal with the political funding cycle in addition to the technology development cycle (still very true).

It’s always been like this “frontier tech “ or “bleeding edge technology” etc…

This is most likely not the final cycle, one where we finally all realize that artificial intelligence is the only technology worth working on and I would be surprised if this is the last “AI bubble.”

The key thing to remember, though is that every AI cycle or AI bubble leads to an entirely evolved set of infrastructure, technologies, and architecture, and ultimately those are the things that matter

Whether or not you make any money is usually the last concern of anyone who’s been working in AI seriously, we’re gonna keep working on AI no matter what.

> The AI bubble is a speculative concept that the AI industry is extremely over-valued. If true, the value of most companies involved in AI (several of whom are worth well over a trillion dollars) will collapse, devastating the entire economy. If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though.

Matteo's analysis is very flawed though. For instance, he projects that the outcome is "devastating the entire economy". Why would that have to be the case though?

The AI bubble can collapse partially. There are tons of examples of how this has happened in the past. Not everything is dot-com 2.0. What we see right now is a "consolidation" bordering on partial collapse of some of the companies' projected revenues. It makes sense to assume that there is not a complete collapse, and some companies will end up dominating more than others.

I think the last paragraph puts it pretty well

>>> As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be. People are afraid of what's going to happen with AI, and rightfully so. Beyond fear for the future, AI in the present has become uncomfortably common, with AI slop everywhere online and increasingly even IRL. This has all happened so fast, it's easy to forget that ChatGPT came out a little less than 4 years ago. Our world has changed in such a scary and odd way, and while I have a pretty optimistic view of AI overall, I get why people would want it all to go away. So, people wishcast. They tell themselves that this is all a giant bubble, and one day soon, everything will crash down and immediately go back to how it used to be.

And on a personal note, this probably goes against all economic theory, but I think the larger the scale gets of money, the less "real" it becomes. The US national debt is $40.5 trillion. I personally don't think a fraction of that will ever really be paid. There are rich and poor, but once you become rich, that added richness is essentially useless, and the debt we see is a mixture of money missing from the poor person's wallet, or the money missing from a billionaire's portfolio. One of these is more sensually palpable than the other.

If your product is good enough, shows potential, and has meaning, it will get funding. I have never done a startup or gotten venture capital so it's pretentious for me to say, but I think the money just comes, through effort (and I think 100's of pitches for the new startup), and we can't always know from where. It's just there. My brain is too small to consider where that money comes from. We're not valuing money at a certain point, but just sheer utility, and so investors will be there to back you up. In decades-long terms, sometimes centuries-long.

The debt will keep building up, but so will be our infrastructural changes. Early adoptees will get rich to degrees, and investors who held a conservative view on major progress like AI (will still be rich but) will be slightly less rich. Maybe there will be unpaid debt, like the 500 billion incurring a $400 billion loss during the dot-com crash. But the technology will continue growing.

After all, money doesn't mean anything anyway (in the theoretical sense). It buys us soup, clothes, and a place to pay rent to, but it is just an agreement. And with the changes in the world economy that some of us are expecting to see after the AI revolution grows even more, I really don't know what the meaning of money will become.

> If you check any online discussion about the financial situation of the AI industry, it's essentially taken for granted that the bubble exists and is going to pop any day now. I don't think that this is a reasonable assumption, though.

To say that it is (essentially) taken for granted isn’t a great start to a rebuke. You have to engage with the arguments that they have, and they have presented arguments. Just see born-again clanker Dan Luu respond to Zitron’s claims.[1]

I don’t see any engagement with skeptic’s arguments in this piece.

[1] https://danluu.com/zitron/

> In other words, there's massive unmet demand for AI companies to profit from.

Of course. There are hundreds of millions of white collar workers that are jealuously hoarding their unrightful wages.

> There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for. You can't really have it both ways here.

But you can. A bubble of this magnitude will negatively impact the world, not just AI investor cretins. You can take the extreme position that AI is useless and still be worried about the fallout.

> It's completely valid to be afraid of AI taking your job, but money is going to change hands when that happens.

The conjunction here implies a contrast which I fail to see.

> As one final note, I don't think the rhetoric about the AI bubble is really about finances. Conversation about the AI bubble is too widespread for it to be a contrarian position, and too gleeful to be driven by investors' fear. More than anything, I think the supposed AI bubble has become such a large talking point because it represents the hope that things can go back to how they used to be. People are afraid of what's going to happen with AI, [...]

The always-amazing observation that your intellectual opponents have motivated reasoning. Likewise, most AI positives have motivated reasoning, like that they can enrich themselves or that they are getting so much code out of their current subscription prices.

When I write about AI it’s clear when I argue against AI itself and when I am whining about my boo-boo thoughts about losing all of my economic prospects.

> I’ve applied to seek the Liberal Party of Canada nomination

That tracks.

blocks.html_en:
Large data centers never made sense. If an additional pc with a graphics card was put into every home, we wouldn't need power grid upgrades. Our power grid is designed around human distribution i.e. homes. Large data centers cherry pick where it may be possible to quickly connect power connections up. Data centers need to secure their power connections before the utility rate hikes on everyone else generate public opposition.

If large data centers cannot secure free power connections paid for by everyone else, they cannot make any of this profitable. The whole thing was a scam from the start. This is why cloud AI companies bought up so much pc and server hardware. Artificial scarcity was the only way to slow down local llm adoption and sell the false narrative that cloud AI has value.

Plucking a graphics card out of every home and centralizing the cards to a handful of large data centers that require a trillion dollars in power grid upgrades is an idea so dumb, we should all be laughing at it. They even have to use active cooling or evaporate drinking water instead of free air cooling. The consumer doesn't benefit in any way from this. Consumers would essentially be paying more just to be datamined.

LLMs are not a bubble, large data centers are a bubble. Look at how large data centers are now the first target in any war. A graphics card in every home, doesn't give someone a concentrated target. National security makes large data centers extremely bad.

blocks.html_en:
Large data centers are dramatically more efficient at utilizing both the power and the hardware.

At it's core, running a top-tier LLM means linear load of trillion+ weights from RAM for every token. The cost of this operation absolutely dwarfs the cost of doing the actual math. If you are only serving a single user, you can only amortize this over a handful of token streams, times like 2-4 for speculative decoding. If you are running in a datacenter, you can batch thousands of streams, and get correspondingly much more tokens out of the same expenditure of energy and hardware.

Be slightly careful with this. Large datacenters use power to operate the facility (this is measured as PUE > 1). Datacenter-oriented hardware often contains low-diameter, high static pressure fans that consume quite impressive amounts of power that are not counted as overhead in the PUE calculation.

A home- or office-oriented workstation will have much less power-hungry fans (go compare a Noctua datasheet to a server fan datasheet - the Noctua wipes the floor with a server fan if measured by CFM/W, and the internal temperature rise is mostly controlled by airflow and not by static pressure). And in some climates and times of year the marginal facility HVAC cost associated with running a computer may be zero or even negative.

And lower utilization hardware may run in on a more efficient point on the power-vs-performance curve. [0]

That being said, your overall point is correct.

[0] For a dramatic demonstration of how much this curve matters, you can run a non-CPU-saturating, non-latency-sensitive workload on various Intel CPUs with and without turbo on. Seeing a 2x or greater difference in reported power is quite possible. (Intel is terribly at writing platform firmware and the default behavior may be wildly suboptimal.)

> There's a weird contradiction you see from AI skeptics where they're afraid of how AI will change the world, but also seem convinced that AI will only ever produce slop that nobody would ever pay money for.

Fair enough. But the real problem, it seems, is that people love slop.

My family is trying to sell a house in the South of France; the real estate people are sending us 500-words emails every so often, that are so obviously AI it hurts. Well written, and content free. Nobody cares. I'm the only one having issues with it.

At work, a new team let Claude do all their work and write all their status reports. Everybody seems to love it. It's so fast! And mostly correct! And so fast to correct when it's wrong! And here too, I'm the only one having issues with it.

A Canadian author wrote a book in French that turned out to be 100% AI ("C'était ça ou mourir"). Before that was revealed, every critic loved it, in Canada, in France and everywhere else (25 translations were started). The public loved it too: it's one of the top best sellers, and success continued even after the "scandal".

We are drowning in slop and nobody cares.

If that's true for every AI output is up for discussion, but it's reasonable that if someone is skeptical about the technology, they will also be skeptical about the quality.

That the tech is taking over many areas is not a stretch at all, that's just something that can be observed. Starts with customer communication as you mentioned, and customer service, and believe it or not I don't think every company should generate their own tech stack and software for their little products.

That does not mean that there can't be good ones too.
